[[steins-gate-worldline|worldline]] structure of the setting — from

existence is only ever inferred from paper trails and secondhand accounts.

appropriate skepticism. #lore

# Episode 01: Turning Point

*Prologue of the Beginning and the End* — the series premiere. A lecture on
time travel, a rooftop satellite, and a pool of blood on the eighth floor of
[[radio-kaikan|the Radio Kaikan building]]. Everything that follows begins here.

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

[[okabe|Rintaro Okabe]] — self-styled mad scientist ==Hououin Kyouma== — drags
[[mayuri|Mayuri Shiina]] to Dr. Nakabachi's press conference on time machine
theory at the [[radio-kaikan|Radio Kaikan]]. Okabe interrupts the lecture to
accuse [[nakabachi|Dr. Nakabachi]] of plagiarizing [[wp:John Titor|John Titor]],
and is pulled out of the hall by a red-haired girl he has never met — who
insists he tried to tell her something *fifteen minutes ago*.

Minutes later, Okabe finds the same girl, [[kurisu|Kurisu Makise]], collapsed
in a pool of blood in an upstairs corridor. Shaken, he texts [[daru|Daru]] from
the street outside — and the world *lurches*. The crowds vanish. Radio Kaikan
now has a crashed satellite embedded in its roof, and according to everyone
else, it has been there since the morning.

:::note
This is the first on-screen worldline shift of the series. Okabe's ability to
retain memories across shifts is later named ==Reading Steiner== — see
[[alpha-worldline#Reading Steiner|the Alpha worldline article]].
:::

Back at the [[future-gadget-lab|Future Gadget Laboratory]], nobody remembers
the press conference — it was cancelled a week ago. Okabe's phone shows the
message to Daru was sent *a week before he wrote it*. And at a later lecture,
Kurisu Makise walks up to him: alive, unstabbed, and very annoyed.

::section[The first D-Mail]{icon="📱"}

The text Okabe sends from outside Radio Kaikan reads, in full:

> Something you should know. Makise Kurisu has been stabbed. I found her body
> on the 8th floor.

Because the [[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave (name subject to change)]] was
running at the moment of transmission, the message arrived on Daru's phone
**a week in the past** — the lab's first D-Mail, sent before anyone knew
D-Mail was possible.[^1] SERN's involvement is not yet visible, but the
IBN 5100 that will dominate the mid-season is already sitting, forgotten, in
the storeroom of the [[yanabayashi-shrine|Yanabayashi Shrine]].

::section[Continuity]{icon="🔗"}

- First appearance of [[okabe]], [[mayuri]], [[daru]], [[kurisu]], and
  [[nakabachi|Dr. Nakabachi]].
- First appearance of the [[future-gadget-lab|Future Gadget Lab]] and FG
  gadget No. 8, the [[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]].
- The metal Upa Mayuri finds at the conference becomes decisive in
  [[episode-22|the finale arc]] — a classic [[wp:Chekhov's gun|Chekhov's gun]].
- Okabe's catchphrase [[el-psy-kongroo]] is spoken four times.

:::collapse{title="Spoilers — what actually happened on the 8th floor"}
The stabbing Okabe witnesses is the event the entire series orbits. The blood
belongs to Kurisu, the assailant is revealed only in the final episodes, and
the "satellite" is Suzuha's time machine. The shift from $0.571024$ to
$0.571015$ happens because Okabe's text — relayed by SERN's echelon logging —
changed which worldline the [[alpha-worldline|Alpha attractor field]]
converged on. See [[steins-gate-worldline#Deceiving the past|Deceiving the past]].
:::

# Episode 02: Time Travel Paranoia

The girl who should be dead walks into the lecture hall. *Time Travel
Paranoia* introduces the series' central question: if the world changed,
why is [[okabe|Okabe]] the only one who noticed?

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

[[kurisu|Kurisu Makise]] corners Okabe after a lecture, demanding to know what
he meant to tell her at Radio Kaikan — a conversation Okabe never had, in
*this* worldline. His frantic reaction ("you should be dead") does not
improve her opinion of him.

Back at the [[future-gadget-lab|lab]], [[daru|Daru]] demonstrates the
[[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]]'s one reliable behavior: bananas placed
inside it turn into an unnatural ==green gel==, and — stranger — the gel
bananas reattach themselves to the bunch left across the room. Okabe starts a
notebook. Column one: *things that should be impossible*.

Meanwhile the @channel boards light up. A poster claiming to be
[[wp:John Titor|John Titor]] — a name Okabe remembers from the year 2000 —
has begun posting *for the first time*, in 2010, describing a dystopian 2036
ruled by SERN and asking for help locating an IBN 5100.

:::warning
Nobody else remembers Titor's 2000 posts. In this worldline they never
happened. Okabe's memory and the world's record now disagree — the first
hard evidence of what the [[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]] will later
quantify.
:::

::::

::section[John Titor's claims]{icon="🕰️"}

:::::tabs
:::tab{label="The 2036 he describes"}
SERN achieved time travel and used it to seize power. A surveillance
dystopia followed. Titor claims to be a resistance courier sent back to
recover an IBN 5100, the only machine able to decode SERN's oldest archives.
:::
:::tab{label="The physics he cites"}
Titor's model matches the [[wp:Many-worlds interpretation|many-worlds
interpretation]] loosely, but with a twist the series makes canonical:
worldlines *converge*. Small changes are absorbed; only changes past a
threshold jump between [[worldlines|attractor fields]]. He calls the constant
measuring this the **divergence number** — see [[divergence-meter]].
:::
::::tab{label="What he gets wrong"}
:::danger
Titor insists time machines cannot cross between attractor fields. Events of
[[episode-22|the finale]] prove this incomplete — the barrier can be crossed,
at a price. Treat his posts as in-universe primary sources, not physics.
:::
::::
:::::

::section[Analysis]{icon="🔬"}

:::figure{align="right" width="260"}
![Gel banana diagram](https://picsum.photos/seed/sg-ep02-gel/260/160 "The gel state: matter after a partial temporal transfer.")
:::

The gel banana is the episode's quiet masterstroke. It establishes — before
any character says "time travel" aloud — that the Phone Microwave transports
matter destructively. The audience is being told, one season early, why a
*human* must never be sent.[^1] When SERN's own experiments surface in
[[episode-03]], the gel state already has a name in the viewer's head.

The divergence reading holds steady at $d=0.571015$ this episode: paranoia,
not physics, is doing the work.

::section[Continuity]{icon="🔗"}

- The IBN 5100 is named for the first time. It resurfaces in
  [[episode-04]], [[episode-05]], and [[episode-08]].
- Kurisu's lecture topic — memory as neural data — foreshadows the
  [[time-leap-machine|Time Leap Machine]] she builds in [[episode-11]].
- Okabe's notebook becomes the seed of the lab's D-Mail log; see
  [[episode-guide#D-Mail record|the D-Mail record]].
- First mention of [[mr-braun|Mr. Braun]], the lab's landlord.

:::collapse{title="Spoilers — Titor's identity"}
The @channel poster is [[suzuha-amane|Suzuha Amane]], posting under her
mission alias. Her father is a lab member. The series does not confirm this
until [[episode-11|Dogma in Event Horizon]].
:::

# Episode 03: Parallel World Paranoia

The episode where the [[future-gadget-lab|Future Gadget Lab]] stops being a
hobby club. A message to the past gets a name, a hack gets an audience, and
SERN gets a reason to notice four amateurs in [[akihabara|Akihabara]].

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

Okabe invites [[kurisu|Kurisu]] to the lab to witness the
[[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]] fire a message into the past. She arrives
prepared to debunk; she leaves having watched a text she wrote appear on a
phone **five days before she wrote it**. Her scientific integrity does the
rest — she cannot walk away from a working time machine, however stupid its
inventors.

[[mayuri|Mayuri]] christens the messages ==D-Mail== (from "DeLorean mail"),
and the lab formalizes its procedure: short messages, timestamped, logged.[^1]

Kurisu identifies the microwave's mechanism as a miniature
[[wp:Kerr black hole|Kerr black hole]] analogue — which should be impossible
at household wattage, unless someone else's experiment is leaking. That
someone is SERN, whose LHC has appeared in every anomalous reading Daru can
find. So [[daru|Daru]] does the obvious thing and hacks SERN.

:::danger
What they find in SERN's internal database — reports titled
[[jellyman-report|"Jellyman's Report"]] — are records of *human* temporal
transfer experiments. Every subject arrived as gel. Every subject was
listed as "material for disposal."
:::

::::

::section[The D-Mail protocol]{icon="📱"}

The rules the lab writes down this episode remain canon for the whole series:

| Rule | Constraint | Discovered |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 36 bytes maximum per D-Mail | [[episode-03]] |
| 2 | Longer messages split and arrive out of order | [[episode-03]] |
| 3 | Receiver's past self reads it as a normal text | [[episode-01]] |
| 4 | Worldline may shift; only Okabe remembers | [[episode-01]] |
| 5 | Microwave must be in operation at send time | [[episode-02]] |

:::tip
36 bytes is 18 full-width Japanese characters — the writers derived every
D-Mail in the series under this budget. Fans check. See the sortable log in
[[episode-guide#D-Mail record|the episode guide]].
:::

::section[The SERN hack]{icon="💻"}

:::figure{align="left" width="260"}
![Terminal screenshot](https://picsum.photos/seed/sg-ep03-hack/260/160 "Daru's proxy chain, dramatized.")
:::

Daru's break-in succeeds because SERN's legacy systems predate modern
encryption — the same reason SERN needs an IBN 5100 to read its *own* oldest
archives. The episode is careful about cause and effect: the lab is not yet
being watched, but the hack writes the first line of the file SERN will
eventually open.

The stolen documents describe "human is dead, mismatch" — the phrase fans
use as shorthand for the gel-transfer failure state.[^2]

```mermaid
graph LR; LHC[SERN LHC] --> DB[(Internal DB)] --> Daru --> Lab[FG Lab]
```

::section[Continuity]{icon="🔗"}

- Kurisu unofficially joins the lab; her badge (Lab Member 004) is issued
  in [[episode-04]].
- First mention of the [[jellyman-report|Jellyman's Report]] by name.
- The 36-byte limit constrains the plots of [[episode-06]], [[episode-08]],
  and [[episode-10]].
- SERN's LHC experiments connect to Titor's 2036 — compare
  [[alpha-worldline#SERN's dystopia|the Alpha worldline article]].

:::collapse{title="Spoilers — why the hack matters"}
SERN's Echelon-style dragnet logs the intrusion. In the
[[alpha-worldline|Alpha attractor field]] this log entry is the proximate
cause of the raid in [[episode-12]], Mayuri's death, and the lab's
destruction. One curious hack, one dead friend — the show's cruelest
cause-and-effect chain.
:::

::section[Quotes]{icon="💬"}

> "It's not paranoia if the world really did change." — Okabe, to no one

> "I'm staying. Not because I believe you. Because I *measured* it." — Kurisu

[^1]: Mayuri's other candidate names included "past mail" (rejected as
      boring) and "OkaMail" (rejected with prejudice).
[^2]: The phrase appears verbatim in the stolen documents; the translation
      wobble is in-universe, from SERN's French-English internal reports.

# Episode 04: Interpreter Rendezvous

Lab Member 004 gets her badge, a journalist who never speaks above a text
message appears, and the hunt for the IBN 5100 begins in earnest.

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

[[kurisu|Kurisu]] accepts a [[lab-member-badge|lab member badge]] — number
004 — with the enthusiasm of a hostage, and immediately proves indispensable
by redesigning the [[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]]'s send procedure so a
D-Mail no longer requires someone to physically kick the microwave door.

Okabe, following [[wp:John Titor|Titor]]'s posts, resolves to find the
IBN 5100 before SERN's collaborators do. The trail leads through
[[akihabara|Akihabara]]'s retro-computing shops to a name Okabe knows:
the [[yanabayashi-shrine|Yanabayashi Shrine]], where a "strange old
computer" was donated decades ago.

At a shop counter he meets [[moeka-kiryu|Moeka Kiryu]], a freelance editor
who communicates almost exclusively by mail even when standing in front of
you — and who is, by coincidence she does not explain, *also* looking for an
IBN 5100.[^1]

:::note
Moeka's mail-only affect reads as comedy on first viewing. On rewatch it is
the episode's loudest alarm. See the spoiler fold below.
:::

The episode's title is literal: everything is interpretation. Moeka
interprets the lab as a lead; Okabe interprets her as a fellow enthusiast;
Kurisu interprets the badge as a joke and pockets it anyway. The script lets
every misreading stand, because on the
[[alpha-worldline|Alpha worldline]] ($d=0.571015$) misreadings are load-bearing:
the truth would end the story here.

no divergence movement — the calm before ==the experiments begin==.

# Episode 05: Starmine Rendezvous

The IBN 5100 comes home to the lab, carried up eight flights of stairs by
four people who have no idea they are carrying the season's fuse.

## Synopsis

Okabe's shrine lead pays off. [[ruka-urushibara|Ruka Urushibara]] — gentle,
soft-spoken, and endlessly patient with Okabe's Hououin Kyouma routine —
retrieves the dusty IBN 5100 from the [[yanabayashi-shrine|Yanabayashi

Getting a 25-kilogram vintage computer across [[akihabara|Akihabara]] and up
to the [[future-gadget-lab|lab]] takes the whole episode's middle act and
most of its comedy budget. [[mr-braun|Mr. Braun]], the landlord, watches them
haul it past his CRT shop and mutters that ==real machines have tubes==.

confirm the worst reading of the [[jellyman-report|Jellyman's Report]]:
SERN has been receiving — and disposing of — human test subjects since
before the lab existed.

:::warning
From this episode on, the lab possesses both halves of a catastrophe:
a working D-Mail device *and* proof of what SERN does to people who have one.

# Episode 06: Butterfly Effect's Divergence

The lab stops observing and starts experimenting. The first *deliberate*
D-Mail is sent, the first worldline shift is engineered on purpose — and
Okabe's lonely superpower finally gets a name.

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

Against [[kurisu|Kurisu]]'s explicit objection ("we understand nothing about
the side effects"), the lab votes to run a controlled test: a D-Mail to
[[daru|Daru]]'s past phone containing a lottery number.[^1]

The send works. The world lurches. And Okabe, alone, remembers the
*previous* version of the evening — the number they chose, the argument, the
pizza. Everyone else remembers having sent a *different* message. The ticket
in Daru's wallet is real, and it is a **losing** ticket: the number arrived
garbled past the 36-byte boundary.

Kurisu names Okabe's cross-worldline memory ==Reading Steiner==, borrowing
the term from Okabe's own chuuni vocabulary, to his enormous satisfaction
and her immediate regret.

Meanwhile [[suzuha-amane|Suzuha Amane]], [[mr-braun|Mr. Braun]]'s new
part-timer, takes an instant, unexplained dislike to Kurisu — and an equally
unexplained interest in whether the lab has "sent anything" yet.

:::note
Suzuha's hostility is the episode's dangling thread. It is not resolved
until [[episode-11]], and the resolution recolors every scene she is in.
:::

::section[Reading Steiner]{icon="🧠"}

The episode gives the series its second pillar (after the D-Mail itself).
The rules, as established here and refined in [[episode-07]]:

- Okabe's memories persist across worldline shifts; his body does not move.
- Everyone else's memories are *rewritten to have always been consistent*
  with the new line.
- The transition is subjectively instant — a lurch, a flicker of vertigo.
- No other confirmed carrier exists on the
  [[alpha-worldline|Alpha attractor field]].[^2]

For the physics-flavored fan theories, see
[[worldlines|the worldline overview]] and
[[alpha-worldline#Reading Steiner|Alpha worldline: Reading Steiner]].

# Episode 07: Divergence Singularity

Everyone wants a D-Mail. The lab grows to six members, the send queue grows
a waiting list, and Okabe begins to notice that every wish granted moves an
invisible number he cannot yet read.

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

Word of the "wish-granting mail" spreads inside the lab's small orbit.
[[faris-nyannyan|Faris]] and [[ruka-urushibara|Ruka]] each quietly ask Okabe
for a send of their own; [[moeka-kiryu|Moeka]] — now Lab Member 005 after a
membership drive Okabe conducts mostly by fiat — asks pointed questions
about the machine's *range*.[^1]

[[kurisu|Kurisu]] formalizes the experiment log and, in the episode's
centerpiece scene, works through the physics on the lab's whiteboard:
if [[wp:John Titor|Titor]]'s attractor-field model is right, the shifts the
lab causes are not branches but **convergences** — the river bends, then
rejoins. Big changes need not big causes but the right *singular points*.

Okabe, the only one who remembers all four worldlines the lab has now
occupied, starts writing his private ledger of differences: which shops
changed names, which posters changed art, who takes sugar now. The scene is
scored like horror, because it is: he is measuring his own drift from
everyone he knows.

:::warning
The lab still has no instrument. The number Okabe is groping for —
divergence — will not be readable until the
[[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]] exists, and the person who builds it
hasn't suffered enough yet to build it.
:::

::section[The whiteboard model]{icon="📐"}

Kurisu's lecture, reproduced by fans from freeze-frames, sketches the
series' cosmology in four claims:

1. Worldlines within an attractor field differ in detail but converge on
   the same major events — $d$ values $0.000000 \le d < 1.000000$ all flow
   to the same 2036.
2. Crossing between fields requires shifting $d$ across an integer
   boundary — an event no D-Mail has yet achieved.
3. Certain events are ==convergence anchors==: they occur on every line of
   a field regardless of intervention.
4. An observer with cross-line memory (Reading Steiner) experiences
   convergence as fate. Everyone else experiences it as *nothing at all*.

```mermaid
graph LR; W1[0.571015] --> C{Anchor}; W2[0.523307] --> C; C --> F[Field future 2036]
```

For the full formalism see [[worldlines|Worldlines]] and the field pages:
[[alpha-worldline|Alpha]], [[beta-worldline|Beta]],
[[steins-gate-worldline|Steins Gate]].

# Episode 08: Chaos Theory Homeostasis I

Moeka's D-Mail goes out, and the single most valuable object in the lab
quietly stops ever having arrived. The Homeostasis trilogy begins.

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

[[moeka-kiryu|Moeka]] finally states her wish: a D-Mail to her own past
phone, about the IBN 5100. She frames it as closure — a message about a
lost opportunity to acquire the machine for her editor. The lab, softened
by weeks of granting smaller wishes, agrees.

Okabe operates the [[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]]. The lurch comes.
And when Reading Steiner clears, Okabe is standing in a
[[future-gadget-lab|lab]] with **no IBN 5100 in it** — a lab where the
shrine storeroom was emptied *before* [[episode-05|the retrieval]], where
[[daru|Daru]]'s SERN decode never finished, and where nobody but Okabe has
ever seen the [[jellyman-report|Jellyman's Report]] in full.

Worse: the divergence reading (reconstructed later — see
[[divergence-meter]]) has moved *down*, to $0.456903$, deeper into the
[[alpha-worldline|Alpha attractor field]].

:::danger
The lab has lost its only means of finishing the SERN decode, and does not
know — cannot know — what Moeka's message actually said. Okabe alone
remembers there ever being something to lose.
:::

Moeka, for her part, reads her own old mail with an unreadable expression,
thanks Okabe politely, and does not come to the lab the next day. Or the
day after.

location, not a feeling. Compare

# Episode 09: Chaos Theory Homeostasis II

Faris's wish rewrites a decade of city planning. Okabe steps out of the lab
into an [[akihabara|Akihabara]] with no maid cafes, no anime billboards, and
no reason to have ever welcomed people like him.

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

[[faris-nyannyan|Faris NyanNyan]] — owner-mascot of
[[may-queen-nyan-nyan|May Queen Nyan-Nyan]] and undefeated champion of the
Rai-Net card scene — asks for her D-Mail: a message to her past self, ten
years back, contents private. Okabe grants it. The lurch comes.

The [[akihabara|Akihabara]] Okabe walks out into is *electronics-district*
Akihabara, the pre-2000s version: gray storefronts, component bins,
no [[may-queen-nyan-nyan|May Queen]], no Rai-Net, no moe culture at all.
Faris's father — dead in every previous line — is alive, and the family's
influence steered the district's development down another path entirely.[^1]

[[mayuri|Mayuri]]'s cosplay circle never formed. [[daru|Daru]]'s favorite
shops never opened. The lab itself survives, but the city around it has
been swapped out from under everyone — and only Okabe grieves a version of
the town that, here, never existed.

:::note
Divergence: $0.456903 \to 0.409431$. The largest *cultural* shift of the
series from the smallest stated wish — the Homeostasis trilogy's thesis in
one move.
:::

completely ordinary message. That is the point.

# Episode 10: Chaos Theory Homeostasis III

The last wish of the trilogy is granted, the divergence number falls to the
bottom of its arc, and Suzuha finally says what she came to say.

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

[[ruka-urushibara|Ruka]]'s wish, carried since [[episode-07]], is the
trilogy's most personal: a D-Mail to Ruka's mother, seventeen years in the
past, about a diet superstition — one said to determine a baby's sex. Okabe
sends it expecting nothing. The lurch says otherwise.

In the new line — divergence $0.337187$, the lowest reading of the entire
[[alpha-worldline|Alpha arc]] — Ruka was born a girl. Nothing else visibly
changes: same shrine, same gentleness, same devotion to Okabe's ridiculous
mentorship. The episode spends its middle act on precisely this stillness,
letting the audience hunt the frame for differences and find only one.

Meanwhile [[suzuha-amane|Suzuha]] quits her job at [[mr-braun|Mr. Braun]]'s
shop, announces she is leaving to "find her father," and asks Okabe to
throw her a farewell party at the [[future-gadget-lab|lab]]. At the party
she almost tells him something — and then the episode's last scene hands
her a reason not to leave at all.[^1]

:::warning
$0.337187$ matters. It is the value fans call ==the floor== — the reading
at which the Alpha field's convergence anchor stops being avoidable by
local moves. See [[alpha-worldline#Divergence readings|the readings table]].

::section[Analysis]{icon="🔬"}

The trilogy closes on its quietest change and its heaviest theme: a wish
that alters a person's entire life story *and changes the worldline less
than a lottery ticket did*. Attractor-field homeostasis is not justice —
it prices what the universe cares about, not what people do.[^2] Ruka's
line becomes the emotional pivot of the undo arc, where Okabe must ask for
each wish back, this one first, from people who have lost nothing they can
remember.

party scene last, after the finale, and it shows.

# Episode 11: Dogma in Event Horizon

Suzuha's identity, the satellite's true nature, and a lecture that turns
memory into cargo. The season's mask comes off in forty minutes of plot
delivered at terminal velocity.

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

The news report that ended [[episode-10]] plays in full: the "satellite" on
[[radio-kaikan|Radio Kaikan]] has been identified by JAXA as *not matching
any launched object*. [[suzuha-amane|Suzuha]] hears it and goes white.

Cornered — gently — by Okabe, she tells the truth: she is a courier from
2036, the [[wp:John Titor|John Titor]] of the @channel posts, and the
object on the roof is her **time machine**, damaged on arrival in the
[[episode-01]] cold open. It travels to the past only. It cannot take her
home. Her mission — recover an IBN 5100, stop SERN's archive from ever
becoming readable *by SERN alone* — has been failing since the machine's
dome cracked.[^1]

Meanwhile [[kurisu|Kurisu]], following the power-draw anomaly filed in
[[episode-08]], presents to the lab the season's second machine: memory
data — roughly 3.24 terabytes per person, she estimates — could be
compressed and sent through the microwave's field **instead of text**. Not
a body. A mind. The [[time-leap-machine|Time Leap Machine]], on a
whiteboard, one week before the lab will need it more than anything.

:::danger
SERN's dragnet flags Kurisu's lecture the night it happens. The lab's
countdown, running silently since [[episode-03|the hack]], has fewer than
two episodes left on it.
:::

::section[The time leap lecture]{icon="🧠"}

Kurisu's proposal, as the lab whiteboards it:

1. A memory is addressable neural state — data, if you can read it.
2. The microwave's field can carry 36 bytes to the past *as text*; with
   SERN's LHC as a relay, bandwidth rises by nine orders of magnitude.
3. 3.24 TB — her estimate for the memories that make a self — fits.[^2]
4. Therefore: send the *mind* of the operator into their own past body.
   No gel. No body at all. A ==time leap==.

:::note
The lecture carefully lists what the leap cannot do: it cannot cross
attractor fields, cannot go forward, and cannot carry anyone but the
operator. All three limits structure the finale arc — see
[[time-leap-machine]] and [[steins-gate-worldline#Operation Skuld|Operation
Skuld]].
:::

- Suzuha's father search resolves next episode; the answer has been a
  named character since [[episode-03]].
- The dome crack from [[episode-01]]'s cold open is finally explained —

- Kurisu's 3.24 TB figure quotes her own memory-topology paper mentioned

which one: not Suzuha's reveal, but the lab *believing* the time leap is
buildable. On every Alpha line where the machine gets built, the raid
follows within days — SERN cannot allow a second party to own working time
travel. The lab crosses the horizon smiling.
:::

# Episode 12: Dogma in Ergosphere

The Time Leap Machine works. SERN knows. The episode the whole Alpha arc
has been pricing finally comes due, and the bill is made out to
[[mayuri|Mayuri Shiina]].

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

Working from [[kurisu|Kurisu]]'s lecture and [[daru|Daru]]'s hijack of
SERN's LHC as a relay, the lab completes the
[[time-leap-machine|Time Leap Machine]] in a montage the score refuses to
celebrate. The device is tested on nothing: Kurisu will not permit a human
trial, and for one afternoon the lab simply *has* a working mind-transfer
device and a party planned for the evening.

The party never happens. [[moeka-kiryu|Moeka]] arrives first — with a
Rounder unit behind her and a gun in her hand. The stolen archive, the
D-Mail logs, the leap machine: SERN wants all of it, and the personnel are
"material." In the raid's held-breath center, Mayuri's pocket watch —
her grandmother's — stops.

Moeka shoots Mayuri. The scene is scored with nothing at all.[^1]

[[suzuha-amane|Suzuha]] crashes through the window a minute too late,
buying Okabe seconds; Kurisu pushes him into the chair of the untested
machine. The last thing Okabe sees on this worldline is
[[future-gadget-lab|his lab]] full of smoke. The last thing he hears is
Kurisu telling him the machine only goes back **48 hours at most**.

:::danger
The leap succeeds. Okabe wakes in his own body, two days earlier, in a
worldline where the raid has not happened yet — and is coming no matter
what he does. Welcome to the mechanism of the next arc.
:::

# Episode 13: Metaphysics Necrosis

__NOTOC__

Two days, on repeat. Okabe spends the episode inside a 48-hour loop trying
to out-position fate with a phone, a bicycle, and a rapidly fraying mind —
and the [[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]] is born from the wreckage.

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

Leap one: Okabe warns nobody, moves [[mayuri|Mayuri]] across town early.
She dies at 19:51 — a traffic accident, streets away from any Rounder.

Leap two: he tells [[kurisu|Kurisu]] everything. They hide Mayuri in
[[akihabara|Akihabara]]'s crowds. 19:51 — a platform surge at the station.
The pocket watch stops first, every time, like a courtesy.[^1]

Leap three, four, five: the episode compresses further attempts into a
montage that the fandom calls the ==necrosis reel==, each loop shot with
one fewer color until the frame is nearly gray. However the day is
arranged, the [[alpha-worldline|Alpha field]] converges. Kurisu — briefed
fresh each loop, believing him faster each time from the detail he
carries — says the quiet part: *the worldline has to change, not the day*.

Between leaps, [[daru|Daru]] and a hollowed-out Okabe begin assembling the
one instrument that could prove it: a meter that reads the divergence
number directly. [[suzuha-amane|Suzuha]] supplies the design — she has
seen one before, she says, in 2036, built by a man she never met.

:::note

confirmation of every reconstructed value this wiki's
[[alpha-worldline#Divergence readings|Alpha readings table]] lists for the

Daru's soldering, [[mr-braun|Mr. Braun]]'s donated tubes.[^2] The
[[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]] converts the arc's invisible
arithmetic into a readable number, and its first reading is a sentence:
$0.337187$, the floor of the field, the number at which Mayuri dies.

The escape threshold, per Suzuha's 2036 intelligence: $d \ge 1.000000$ —
the [[beta-worldline|Beta attractor field]]. No D-Mail the lab has sent
moved the line more than $0.07$. They sent six.

  [[episode-10]], [[episode-09]], [[episode-08]] — in reverse order, each
  one a person's wish taken back.
- The meter's 2036 original and its unnamed builder are resolved in
  [[episode-22|the finale]].
- Loop 3 gives Moeka her first post-raid characterization; her arc
  continues in [[episode-14]].

Episodes 13–16 all carry "Necrosis" titles: the death is Okabe's Alpha-arc
self. The man who leaps out of episode 16 is not the man who leapt into
episode 13, and the show means the word clinically — tissue that will not

# Episode 14: Physically Necrosis

The undo arc begins. To climb out of the Alpha field's floor, Okabe must
take back the wishes his lab granted — starting with the one whose
beneficiary lost nothing and gained a life: [[ruka-urushibara|Ruka]].

:::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
::::column

## Synopsis

Armed with the [[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]] and Suzuha's
threshold ($d \ge 1.000000$, the [[beta-worldline|Beta field]]), Okabe
maps the road out: undo the D-Mails in reverse. Last sent, first
unsent — [[episode-10|Ruka's]], then [[episode-09|Faris's]], then
[[episode-08|Moeka's]], the one that took the IBN 5100 and armed SERN.

The mechanics are ugly. A D-Mail cannot be *recalled*; it must be
**countermanded** — a second message that convinces the past to act as if
the first never arrived. And the sender's consent matters: these are
people's wishes, not Okabe's to revoke by stealth.[^1]

So Okabe asks. The episode's long, quiet center is Okabe explaining to
Ruka — who remembers no other life — that a version of the world exists
where Ruka was born a boy, that Mayuri dies on every line of *this*
world, and that he has no right to ask what he is asking. Ruka listens.
Ruka asks one question: **"In that world — was I still your apprentice?"**

The answer is yes. The consent is given before the sentence ends.

:::danger
The countermand goes out at 19:40. The lurch comes. The meter, in the
episode's final shot, reads $0.409431$ — one rung up the ladder, thirteen
episodes of consequences to climb back through.
:::

::::

::::column

| Air date | 2010-07-06 |
| Arc | [[episode-guide#The undo arc\|Undo arc]] |

| Shift to | [[alpha-worldline\|Alpha]] $0.409431$ |
| Countermanded | Ruka's D-Mail ([[episode-10\|ep. 10]]) |
| Consent given by | [[ruka-urushibara\|Ruka]] |

:::

::::

:::::

::section[The ladder]{icon="🪜"}

```mermaid
graph LR; A[0.337187] -->|undo Ruka| B[0.409431] -->|undo Faris| C[0.456903] -->|undo Moeka| D[0.523307] -.->|?| E[1.000000+]
```

| Step | Countermand | Restores | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ruka's mail | This episode's climb | A life story |
| 2 | Faris's mail | Otaku [[akihabara\|Akihabara]] | Her father, again |
| 3 | Moeka's mail | The IBN 5100 trail | *See spoiler fold* |
| 4 | The first D-Mail | [[episode-01\|Ep. 01]]'s message | Everything else |

:::warning
Step 4 is the arc's buried lede: the ladder's top rung is Okabe's own
accidental D-Mail from [[episode-01]] — and undoing a message that reads
"Makise Kurisu has been stabbed" means restoring the timeline where the
stabbing *matters*. The meter can reach $1.000000$; the price is posted at
[[beta-worldline|the Beta worldline article]].
:::

::section[Consent as mechanic]{icon="🤝"}

The episode formalizes the undo arc's moral engine. Compare the trilogy
and its mirror:

| Wish granted | Wish revoked | Symmetry |
|---|---|---|
| [[episode-10\|Ep. 10]] — Ruka, silently happy | Ep. 14 — Ruka, knowingly grieving | Same shrine steps, same framing |
| [[episode-09\|Ep. 09]] — Faris's private text | Undone with her hand on the send key | Her choice, both times |
| [[episode-08\|Ep. 08]] — Moeka's hidden order | The arc's hardest ask | *Fold below* |

:::collapse{title="Spoilers — Moeka's countermand"}
Moeka's mail cannot be countermanded by persuasion — she is a Rounder and
the mail was her mission. The arc routes through her handler "FB," whose
identity is the mid-season's last twist: the shop below the lab was never
just a shop. [[mr-braun|Mr. Braun]]'s tubes were in the
[[divergence-meter|meter]] all along.
:::

::section[Analysis]{icon="🔬"}

:::figure{align="right" width="260"}
![Shrine steps at dusk](https://picsum.photos/seed/sg-ep14-shrine/260/160 "The same steps as episode 10, lit for grief instead of stillness.")
:::

"Physically Necrosis" completes the season's thesis statement: time travel
in this story is not a physics problem but a consent problem. Every rung
of the ladder is a conversation, and the meter's rising digits — $0.337$,
$0.409$, onward toward $1.048596$ and the
[[steins-gate-worldline|Steins Gate worldline]] — measure not energy but
forgiveness granted.[^2]

::section[Continuity]{icon="🔗"}

- The reverse-order rule is Suzuha's contribution, from watching SERN
  unwind resistance operations in 2036.
- Ruka's apprentice question echoes the pose scene from [[episode-05]].
- The meter's digits appear in the OP from this episode onward — the
  production's own spoiler, hidden at 24 frames per second.

[^1]: Kurisu's rule, stated over Okabe's objection and adopted into lab
      law: "You don't get to edit people back for your own convenience."
[^2]: The staff commentary on the home release uses almost this exact
      phrase, which the wiki notes with some smugness.

# Getting Started

Welcome! This page covers how to write for this wiki. See also [[index|the main page]],
and the **Syntax guide** (book icon in the toolbar, or `Alt+G`) for a copyable
reference of everything below.

## Writing basics

Open any page from the sidebar. The editor supports standard markdown plus wiki extras:

- **Bold**, *italic*, ~~strikethrough~~, ==highlights==, and inline #wiki tags
- `inline code` and code blocks
- Tables, blockquotes, links, footnotes[^1]
- Images — paste one straight into the editor and it uploads itself
- Wikilinks: `[[Page Name]]`, or `[[Page Name#Heading|Label]]` for a section —
  like [[getting-started#writing-basics|this one]]. A red link means the page
  doesn't exist yet.

[^1]: Like this footnote.

## Page metadata

Start a page with a frontmatter block to control how it appears in listings:

```yaml
---
title: Display Name
categories: [Characters]
aliases: [Old Name]
sortKey: Name
---
```

`[[Category:Some Category]]` anywhere in the body also files the page into a
category — it's hidden in the rendered article and shows in the Categories bar
at the foot of the page.

## Structure and layout

- `:::infobox{title="…" image="…"}` — the right-rail card you see on [[okabe|character pages]]
- `::::columns{ratio="65-35"}` with `:::column` fences — multi-column pages ([[layout-demo|demo]])
- `::section[Title]{icon="📘"}` — decorated section bands for portals
- `::category-index{of="Characters"}` — automatic A–Z listings ([[appendix|demo]])
- `{{Template|param=value}}` — reusable content from `_templates/` ([[templates-demo|demo]])

If you misspell a directive, the preview shows a warning box where it would
have rendered — nothing fails silently.

## Publishing workflow

| Action | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+S` / Save | Commits to your personal draft branch |
| Publish | Opens a pull request: draft → main |
| Merge PR | Publishes the change to the live wiki |

Saving never touches the live branch directly — every change goes through a
draft, so nothing breaks the wiki mid-edit.

## Local dev mode

Running with `VITE_DEV_MODE=local` serves this `dev-content/` folder from disk
with no GitHub auth; branches and PRs are simulated in memory.

```bash
pnpm install
VITE_DEV_MODE=local pnpm dev
```

## Theming

Open the **Theme** panel in the toolbar to switch presets (Archive, Fandom
Gold, Midnight Blue, Light, Slate Dark), adjust colors, fonts, and content
width, or set a background image. Themes live in `_config/theme.json`, so they
publish like any other edit.

# Akihabara

:::infobox{title="Akihabara" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/akiba-town/300/180" caption="Electric Town. Every timeline agrees on the neon."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Type | District |
| City | Tokyo, Chiyoda ward |
| Nicknames | Akiba, Electric Town |
| Character | Electronics, otaku culture, back-alley salvage |
| Key sites | [[radio-kaikan\|Radio Kaikan]], [[akihabara-station\|Akihabara Station]], [[braun-tube-workshop\|Braun Tube Workshop]], [[may-queen-nyan-nyan\|May Queen Nyan-Nyan]] |
| Lab presence | [[future-gadget-lab\|Future Gadget Laboratory]] |
| Worldline sensitivity | Extreme (see below) |
| SERN activity | Historical surveillance confirmed |
| Best crepes | Disputed; see talk page |
:::

**Akihabara** — *Akiba* to everyone who has been twice — is Tokyo's
electric town: a district of component shops, anime storefronts, maid
cafes, and arcades stacked vertically until the signage becomes the
architecture. It is the home ground of the
[[future-gadget-lab|Future Gadget Laboratory]] and the stage for nearly
every event this wiki documents. When worldlines shift, ==Akihabara is
where the difference shows first== — and in one infamous case, the
district itself was the difference.

::section[Character]{icon="🏮"}

::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
:::column
Akiba runs on two economies. Above ground: flagship stores, character
goods, billboards that replace themselves seasonally, the crowd flowing
from [[akihabara-station|the station]] down Chuo-dori on foot when the
street closes to cars. Below the signage: the older metabolism of
component stalls and junk shops — bins of salvaged capacitors, one-man
counters that can source a vacuum tube discontinued before the customer
was born. The [[future-gadget-lab|lab]] is a creature of the second
economy; the [[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]]'s Nixie tubes, the
[[future-gadget-02|Helicam]]'s camera, and most of the FG line's organs
were bought within a ten-minute radius of its door.

The district's texture is why the lab could exist unnoticed for so long:
in Akihabara, a person carrying a raygun-shaped remote control and
twenty meters of coolant hose is ==below the threshold of remark==.
:::
:::column
**Lab supply radius**

- Nixie tubes — back-alley stall, 4 min
- IR LEDs, bulk — 2 min
- Loc-line hose — 6 min
- Glow fluid — party supplier, 9 min
- Courage — [[may-queen-nyan-nyan|May
  Queen]], 3 min
:::
::::

::section[Worldline sensitivity]{icon="🌀"}

Akihabara's present character is *recent* — a layer of otaku commerce
deposited over an older radio-parts district in a single generation. This
made it terrifyingly responsive to D-Mail interference. The lab's
documented worldline shifts altered, at various divergence values: which
stores anchored which corners, whether a landmark
[[radio-kaikan|building]] bore a satellite through its roof, and — at the
deepest recorded excursion — ==whether the otaku layer had happened at
all==. On the 0.33-band worldline, lab members walked out into an
Akihabara of gray electronics wholesalers, the moe signage gone as if
scrubbed, and understood viscerally what the
[[attractor-field|attractor field]] pages mean by "detail." See
[[episode-12|Episode 12]].

| Divergence band | Akihabara's state | Witness |
|---|---|---|
| 0.33 | Radio-town only; otaku culture absent | [[okabe\|Okabe]] |
| 0.40–0.57 | Familiar Electric Town, minor storefront drift | Lab consensus |
| 1.04 ([[steins-gate-worldline\|SG]]) | Familiar, plus one impossible satellite | Everyone, finally |
| 1.13 | Familiar; military presence in later years | See [[beta-worldline]] |

:::warning
Wiki policy: statements about "current" Akihabara storefronts must cite a
divergence value. The edit war this rule ended is preserved in the page
history as a cautionary exhibit.
:::

::section[Sites of interest]{icon="📍"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Landmarks"}
[[radio-kaikan|Radio Kaikan]] — the district's vertical heart and the
site of the story's inciting impossibility. [[akihabara-station|Akihabara
Station]] — everyone's entrance and several partings. The riverside
walk toward [[yanabayashi-shrine|Yanabayashi Shrine]], where the noise
falls away block by block.
:::
:::tab{label="Daily life"}
The [[braun-tube-workshop|Braun Tube Workshop]] with the
[[future-gadget-lab|lab]] above it; [[may-queen-nyan-nyan|May Queen
Nyan-Nyan]], the maid cafe where half the lab's meetings actually happen;
the vending machine corner that has sold Dk Pepper on every recorded
worldline, a constancy lab members find genuinely comforting. #lore
:::
:::tab{label="Vanished"}
Storefronts that exist only in [[reading-steiner|one man's memory]]: a
crepe stand, a rental showcase shop, an arcade with exactly one good
cabinet. Okabe's list is in the lab notebook under "places I owe money
in worldlines that no longer exist."
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="A word on crowds"}
Akiba's crowd is the lab's camouflage and its dread. Every SERN tail was
lost in it; one was *spotted* because he stood still in it, which nobody
in Akihabara does. The [[lab-member-handbook|handbook]]'s tradecraft
section is one line: "Move like you're late for a preorder."
:::

::section[See also]{icon="🔗"}

The real district that lends this one its wattage is documented at
[[wp:Akihabara]]. Within this wiki, Akihabara is less a setting than a
==barometer== — check any event page's divergence value, then check what
the neon was doing. The unwritten survey
[[akihabara-storefront-concordance|storefront concordance]] remains
red-linked and, honestly, may defeat whoever attempts it.

The **Future Gadget Laboratory** is a rented second-floor walkup in
[[akihabara|Akihabara]] where [[okabe|Rintaro Okabe]] and a small,
fiercely loyal membership build joke inventions — and where, in the summer
everything changed, they accidentally built the world's second time
machine. It is a clubroom, a workshop, a safehouse, and at various points
a battlefield; the [[episode-guide|episode guide]] barely leaves it for
whole stretches, because for this story the lab *is* the world.

::section[Premises]{icon="🏠"}

::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
:::column
The lab occupies one open room plus a kitchenette, a bathroom, and a
steep stair to the roof. Furnishing is archaeological: a sagging sofa
(sleep rated, two persons, diagonal), the main workbench, a CRT
television that predates most members, and shelving whose lower strata
have not been observed since founding. The [[phone-microwave|PhoneWave]]
holds the kitchenette counter; the [[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]]
sits on the anomaly shelf beside the [[gel-banana|sealed specimens]]; the
wall hooks hold [[future-gadget-01|FG #1]] and whichever umbrella nobody
has reclaimed.

Below, at street level, hums the [[braun-tube-workshop|Braun Tube
Workshop]], whose proprietor doubles as landlord and involuntary
first-responder to everything the lab drops, floods, or detonates. The
relationship is best described as ==weaponized patience==, in both
directions.
:::

**Lab member roster**

- 001 — [[okabe|Rintaro Okabe]]
- 002 — [[mayuri|Mayuri Shiina]]
- 003 — [[daru|Itaru Hashida]]
- 004 — [[kurisu|Kurisu Makise]]
- 005–008 — see
  [[lab-member-handbook#roster|handbook roster]]

::section[A tour]{icon="🚪"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Main room"}
Workbench, sofa, CRT, whiteboard bearing the [[attractor-field|valley
diagram]] in its fourth redrawing and one corner of ink that doesn't
erase. The floor's center is kept clear by standing order — a habit from
the [[future-gadget-02|Helicam]] era that outlived the flights.

:::

Alexis Leskinen is a professor of cognitive science at
[[viktor-chondria-university|Viktor Chondria University]], director of its
[[strategic-focus-lab|Strategic Focus Laboratory]], and the co-creator —
with [[maho-hiyajo|Maho Hiyajo]] and the late [[kurisu|Kurisu Makise]]'s
research legacy — of **Amadeus**, an AI built from a digitized human
memory-model. On the [[beta-worldline|Beta worldline]] where [[okabe|
Okabe]] has abandoned time travel, Leskinen arrives in [[akihabara|
Akihabara]] wearing the friendly face of the story's next disaster.

::section[Amadeus]{icon="🤖"}

:::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
::::column
The [[amadeus-system|Amadeus system]] instantiates a person's archived
memories as an interactive agent — in the famous case, Kurisu's, taken
from a research snapshot months before her death. The scientific claim is
careful: Amadeus *models* memory, it does not host a soul. The dramatic
claim is less careful, because Okabe cannot tell the difference across a
phone screen, and neither, for long stretches, can the audience.[^turing]

Leskinen's genius was never the neuroscience — that was Kurisu's and
Maho's. It was recognizing what a memory-model is *worth*, and to whom.
::::
::::column
:::note
The professor's beloved catchphrase-English ("Fantastic!") and his habit
of losing drinking contests to Maho are, per the spoiler section, some of
the most effective cover ever written into this franchise.
:::
::::
:::::

::section[The reveal]{icon="🕶️"}

:::collapse{title="Spoilers: Steins;Gate 0's true antagonist"}
Leskinen runs a [[stratfor-echelon|Stratfor-linked]] intelligence cell
inside VCU. The Strategic Focus Laboratory is exactly what its name says
— a targeting apparatus — and Amadeus was funded as an interrogation and
succession tool: a way to keep exploiting a scientist's mind after the
scientist is gone. On the worst Beta branches he personally oversees
[[kagari-shiina|Kagari Shiina's]] conditioning, and his cheerful lecture
manner does not change one degree while doing it. The kindly-professor
performance is total; the wiki's editors call him the franchise's answer
to the question "what if SERN were charming?" #lore
:::

::section[Across the worldlines]{icon="🌐"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Beta"}
Fully active: Amadeus launches, the war clock runs, and Leskinen's cell
races Russia for the Makise legacy with Okabe in the crossfire.
:::
:::tab{label="Alpha"}
Never appears — SERN's monopoly on time-travel research leaves nothing
for rival programs to chase. His absence from Alpha branches is itself a
data point about how the [[divergence-meter|divergence]] structure gates
the cast.
:::
:::tab{label="Steins;Gate"}
A genuinely great teacher at VCU whose star pupil, one K. Makise,
politely declines every defense-adjacent grant he brings her. Fantastic.
:::
::::

::section[Assessment]{icon="🧪"}

:::warning
Editors: keep the friendly-professor sections of this page *accurate to
the performance*. The page used to editorialize every scene with "(this
was fake)" and it read terribly; the reveal section exists so the rest of
the article doesn't have to flinch. The same policy applies on
[[yuugo-tennouji|Mr. Braun's]] page, for the same structural reason —
this franchise loves a warm double agent. #lore
:::

His drinking-contest losses to [[maho-hiyajo|Maho]] — a woman half his
mass — remain unexplained by the text. The wiki's two standing theories:
he throws them to build rapport, or Finnish-American folklore about
professors is simply wrong. Divergence between the theories:
$\Delta \approx$ unmeasurable; both are in character.

| | |

| Confirmed appearances | Zero — see authenticity note |
| Status | Unknown; presumed active ([[alpha-worldline\|Alpha]]) |
:::

Daigo Fubuki, codename **F1**, is the reconstructed identity of the
[[rounders|Rounders]] field commander for the Far East sector — the tier
of the hierarchy *above* the handlers, the man to whom "FB" reported. He
never appears on screen. His existence is inferred entirely from the
recovered message logs of the people beneath him, which makes this page
the wiki's most heavily disclaimed biography and, editors would argue,
its most honest picture of how [[sern|SERN]] actually works.

:::warning
**Authenticity note.** Every fact on this page is a reconstruction from
the FB message archive and two SOC routing headers recovered in
[[operation-verdandi]]. The name "Daigo Fubuki" itself may be another
alias in a chain of them. Treat the infobox as a hypothesis with a
picture. #lore #stub
:::

::section[The collector]{icon="🗄️"}

F1's traffic shows one obsession: vintage computers. The IBN 5100
retrieval order that drives half the Alpha arc originates from his desk,
but it sits in a longer pattern — recovered manifests show SOC teams
quietly acquiring pre-1980 hardware across three continents since at
least 2005.[^manifest] The lab's eventual theory: [[sern|SERN]] was not
looking for *the* IBN 5100. It was looking for ==all of them==, because
any surviving unit could decode what the lab decoded.

| Order date | Item class | Sector | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2005-11 | IBN 5100 (2 units) | Western Europe | Acquired |
| 2007-03 | IBN 5100 (1 unit) | North America | Acquired |
| 2008-06 | Peripheral archive, IBN series | Far East | Partial |
| 2010-07 | IBN 5100 (1 unit) — the [[akihabara\|Akihabara]] order | Far East | **Failed** |

The single failure on the table is the plot of the series.

::section[Command style]{icon="📡"}

:::::columns{ratio="55-45"}
::::column
Read end to end, F1's side of the FB correspondence is a portrait of
institutional evil at its most banal: no threats, no ideology, just
deadlines. Assets are "inventory." The order to cut [[moeka-kiryu|M4]]
loose is eleven words long and misspells her codename. The wiki
reproduces none of the messages directly — the archive's legal status is
disputed — but the pattern they document is why this page exists.
::::
::::column
:::danger
On [[alpha-worldline|Alpha]] branches that reach 2036, SOC routing
headers place F1's successor organization inside the occupation
government's registry directorate. The Rounders never disband; they get
promoted. See [[suzuha-amane|Suzuha's]] page for the world that follows.
:::
::::
:::::

Faris NyanNyan — legal name **Rumiho Akiha** — is the star waitress of the
[[mayqueen-nyannyan|MayQueen NyanNyan]] maid café, Lab Member No. 007, and,
behind the cat-ear persona, the heiress of the family that owns most of the
land under [[akihabara|Akihabara]]. The district's transformation into an
otaku capital was, in large part, a decision she made as a grieving child
with a controlling interest; the moe economy of an entire city block is
downstream of one girl's coping mechanism.[^district]

::section[Two names]{icon="🎭"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Faris"}
The public self: relentlessly cheerful, fluent in the maid-café idiom she
largely invented, and a national-class player of the collectible card game
*Rai-Net Access Battlers*. "Faris" is not a mask so much as a renovation —
she built the persona at age eleven and moved in permanently.
:::
:::tab{label="Rumiho"}
The private self appears rarely: in board meetings of
[[akiha-cyber-solutions|ACS]] she attends by proxy, in the anniversary of
her father's death, and in the handful of scenes where [[okabe|Okabe]]
needs the person rather than the performance. Rumiho speaks without the
"nya." It is always slightly alarming.
:::
::::

::section[The D-Mail]{icon="📨"}

Faris's [[phone-microwave|D-Mail]] is one of the story's cleanest
demonstrations of worldline mechanics: a single message to the past —
warning her father not to board a plane in 2001 — and [[akihabara|
Akihabara]] itself transforms. On the resulting branch her father lives,
the moe district never happens, the [[radio-kaikan|Radio Kaikan]] hosts
appliance vendors instead of card tournaments, and the IBN 5100 the lab
desperately needs follows a completely different chain of custody.[^ibn]

:::warning
Undoing this D-Mail is among the hardest things [[okabe|Okabe]] does in the
Alpha arc — not technically, but because it requires asking a daughter to
re-consent to her father's death. See [[episode-17]]. Divergence delta for
the branch: $|\Delta d| \approx 0.075$. #lore
:::

::section[Capabilities]{icon="🧪"}

:::::columns{ratio="55-45"}
::::column
It is easy to forget, amid the cat ears, that Faris is one of the most
strategically capable people in the cast. She reads the Rai-Net board the
way [[kurisu|Kurisu]] reads a journal paper, she reads *people* better
than anyone in the lab, and she deduced Okabe's time-travel secret from
behavioral evidence alone — then pretended she hadn't, to spare him the
explanation, nya.
::::
::::column
:::tip
Her Rai-Net national title is not flavor text: in [[episode-11]] the
championship bracket becomes, briefly and absurdly, the fulcrum of a
worldline. Watch her hands in that episode — the animators gave her a
tell.
:::

# Judy Reyes

:::infobox{title="Judy Reyes" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/judy-reyes/300/180" caption="The Amadeus project's conscience, by her own job description."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Position | Research ethicist, [[viktor-chondria-university\|VCU]] |
| Assigned to | [[amadeus-system\|Amadeus]] oversight board |
| Laboratory | [[strategic-focus-lab\|Strategic Focus Laboratory]] (external reviewer) |
| Doctorate | Philosophy of mind, VCU 2004 |
| Known for | The "Reyes Criteria" for memory-model consent |
| Colleagues | [[maho-hiyajo\|Maho Hiyajo]] · [[alexis-leskinen\|Alexis Leskinen]] |
| Status | Alive ([[beta-worldline\|Beta]]); unverified elsewhere |
:::

Judy Reyes is the research ethicist attached to [[viktor-chondria-university|
Viktor Chondria University's]] [[amadeus-system|Amadeus]] project — the
person whose signature was required, and obtained, before a dead woman's
memories were switched on and asked how they felt today. A minor figure
in the Beta arc's background, she has become a fixture of the fandom's
supplementary-material deep dives, because her audit memos, glimpsed on
screen for single frames, reward pausing.[^frames]

::section[The Reyes Criteria]{icon="⚖️"}

Her published framework for memory-model research asks three questions of
any Amadeus-class instantiation, and the show quietly grades its cast
against them:

| Criterion | Amadeus-Kurisu | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Did the source consent to instantiation? | Research-archive clause, signed at 17 | Technically |
| Can the instance refuse interaction? | Sessions are operator-initiated | No |
| Who may terminate, and on what grounds? | [[strategic-focus-lab\|SFL]] directorate, at discretion | The problem |

The third row is the arc's ethical hinge: ==everyone who loves the
instance has no authority over it, and everyone with authority does not
love it==.

::section[In the story]{icon="🎬"}

:::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
::::column
Reyes appears in three scenes and is consequential in one: the December
board meeting where she files a formal objection to session-frequency
limits being waived for "priority users" — the waiver that permits
[[okabe|Okabe's]] marathon conversations with the Kurisu instance. Her
objection is overruled by [[alexis-leskinen|Leskinen]] in forty seconds
of screen time. On rewatch, knowing his agenda, the scene plays as a
security officer disabling an alarm.
::::
::::column
:::note
Whether Reyes suspected the SFL's covert program is unresolved. Her
resignation letter, dated the week of the Amadeus shutdown, surfaced in
supplementary materials with one line highlighted: "I was asked to
review a system. I was never permitted to review its purpose."
:::
::::
:::::

::section[Assessment]{icon="🧪"}

The wiki files Reyes as the Beta arc's answer to a question the Alpha arc
never thought to ask: what would it look like if an institution *tried*
to do this responsibly? Her criteria are sound, her process is honest,
and none of it matters, because process cannot bind the people who fund
it. She is [[sern|SERN's]] photographic negative — no conspiracy, no
malice, total procedural correctness, same result.

- Author, *Consent Beyond the Grave: Memory Models and the Research
  Subject* (VCU Press, 2008) — see [[wp:Philosophy of mind]] for the
  tradition she writes in.
- Her oversight files on [[kagari-shiina|the Shiina case]] have never
  been recovered. #wip #lore

[^frames]: The pause-worthy memos appear in [[episode-05]] and
    [[episode-09]] of Steins;Gate 0; transcriptions live at
    [[amadeus-audit-memos]].

Kagari Shiina is a war orphan from the [[beta-worldline|Beta worldline's]]
ruined future, adopted there by an adult [[mayuri|Mayuri Shiina]] and sent
back to 1998 aboard the resistance's second time machine. The insertion
goes wrong; the lab meets her twelve years later as an amnesiac young
woman in 2010 [[akihabara|Akihabara]] who remembers nothing but a fragment
of melody — a lullaby Mayuri has hummed since childhood.

::section[The lost years]{icon="🧩"}

Between 1998 and 2010 Kagari's trail goes almost completely dark; the wiki
reconstructs it from the Beta arc's worst reveals. The short version: a
child with no records, no guardian, and a time machine's residue on her
clothes does not stay unnoticed by the kind of institutions that watch for
exactly that.[^trail]

:::collapse{title="Spoilers: what the Strategic Focus Lab did"}
Kagari's amnesia is not trauma alone — it is product. The
[[strategic-focus-lab|SFL]] program under [[alexis-leskinen|Leskinen]]
identified her as time-machine debris and spent years conditioning her as
a sleeper asset, using the [[amadeus-system|Amadeus]] tooling in reverse:
instead of instantiating a recorded mind, ==overwriting a live one==. The
lullaby is the seam where the overwrite failed. Every scene where she
hums it is the real Kagari surfacing, which reframes the entire arc on
rewatch and is the reason this wiki's editors consider her the Beta
storyline's most quietly horrifying element. #lore
:::

::section[Mother and daughter]{icon="🎀"}

:::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
::::column
The heart of Kagari's story is anachronistic: she is the adopted daughter
of a Mayuri who does not exist yet, meeting the eighteen-year-old who will
become her. The 2010 Mayuri, without a word of the future explained to
her, simply *behaves like her mother* — same warmth, same stubbornness on
exactly one subject at a time — and Kagari's conditioning erodes against
it. The show's thesis in miniature: identity is not storage, it is
practice.
::::
::::column
:::warning
Her resemblance to [[kurisu|Kurisu]] is never canonically resolved.
Theories are catalogued at [[kagari-resemblance-theories]]; the wiki
endorses none of them. #wip
:::
::::
:::::

::section[Timeline]{icon="🗓️"}

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| ~2029 | Born amid the war ([[beta-worldline\|Beta]] future) |
| 2036 | Adopted by Mayuri Shiina |

::section[The lullaby]{icon="🎼"}

The melody itself — four bars, minor key, resolving on an unresolved
fourth — appears in the score every time conditioning and memory fight
for the same body. Musicologically-minded fans have transcribed it and
noted that Mayuri hums it fractionally differently in 2010 than adult
Mayuri does in 2036 flashbacks: the 2036 version is the *taught* version,
smoothed by repetition to a child. The 2010 version still has the
hesitation in bar three. Kagari, devastatingly, hums the smoothed one.[^hum]

:::tip
First-time viewers should not look up the lullaby's title — it is named
on screen only at the arc's climax, and the name is a spoiler in four
syllables.
:::

# Luka Urushibara

:::infobox{title="Luka Urushibara" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/luka-urushibara/300/180" caption="Miko-in-training at Yanabayashi Shrine."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Home | Yanabayashi Shrine, [[akihabara\|Akihabara]] backstreets |
| Role | Shrine keeper's child; miko-in-training |
| Lab member | No. 006 |
| Mentor (self-appointed) | [[okabe\|"Hououin Kyouma"]] |
| Weapon | Replica katana, "Samidare" |
| Guardian of | A certain shrine storeroom relic |
| Gender | Male (Beta) \| female (post-D-Mail Alpha branch) |
| Height | 159 cm |
| Status | Alive (all known worldlines) |
:::

Luka Urushibara is the gentle, perpetually apologizing child of the
Yanabayashi Shrine's keeper, [[okabe|Okabe's]] most devoted disciple in the
Hououin Kyouma fiction, and Lab Member No. 006. Their family shrine sits a
few streets from the [[future-gadget-lab|lab]], and its storeroom turns out
to hold one of the most important objects in the entire story — the IBN
5100, donated years earlier and forgotten under a tarp.[^relic]

::section[The D-Mail]{icon="📨"}

Luka's [[phone-microwave|D-Mail]] is the story's most intimate use of the
technology: a message sent back seventeen years asking their mother to eat
differently during pregnancy — folk-science, but on a worldline where it
worked. The resulting branch rewrites Luka's sex at birth, and with it a
thousand small social frictions the original Luka had carried quietly for
a lifetime.

:::warning
As with [[faris-nyannyan|Faris's]] branch, undoing this D-Mail in
[[episode-16]] required its sender's consent — a scene widely considered
the emotional center of the Alpha arc's back half. Handle spoilers gently
on this page. #lore
:::

:::collapse{title="Spoilers: the day that gets undone"}
On the branch being erased, Luka finally asks Okabe for the one thing the
worldline made possible, and gets a single day's answer before the reset.
The kindness of the writing is that the day still happened: Reading
Steiner or no, Luka chooses the original worldline knowingly, trading the
life for the shrine's relic and the lab's survival. Okabe, who remembers
everything, never once mentions it. Neither does Luka — but on every
branch afterward, Samidare's practice swings start at dawn instead of noon.
:::

::section[Swordsmanship]{icon="⚔️"}

:::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
::::column
Under Okabe's flamboyant, largely fraudulent instruction, Luka practices a
sword style Okabe invented and named "Kyouma-ryu." What neither of them
expected is that Luka got *good* — the timid posture disappears the moment
the replica blade comes out, and in the [[beta-worldline|Beta worldline's]]
darker hours that skill stops being a joke entirely.
::::
::::column
:::note
The katana "Samidare" is shrine property, technically an offering, and
absolutely not supposed to leave the grounds. It has left the grounds in
every single worldline on record.
:::
::::
:::::

::section[Relationships]{icon="🤝"}

| Person | Relation |
|---|---|
| [[okabe\|Rintaro Okabe]] | Master, in the theatrical sense; anchor, in the real one |
| [[mayuri\|Mayuri Shiina]] | Fits Luka for cosplay; the shrine's most frequent visitor |
| [[faris-nyannyan\|Faris NyanNyan]] | Fellow "confidant" of Kyouma's inner circle |
| Father (Yanabayashi keeper) | Stern, devout, and the reason the IBN 5100 was preserved |
| [[kurisu\|Kurisu Makise]] | Awkward mutual respect after the events of [[episode-16]] |

::section[The shrine]{icon="⛩️"}

Yanabayashi Shrine is small, old, and — by the standards of a district
that rebuilt itself around electronics twice in a century — almost
defiantly analog. Its storeroom ledger, maintained by hand since 1962,
is the document that eventually lets the lab trace the IBN 5100's
donation history across worldline branches, making one dusty notebook
briefly the most strategically important text in [[akihabara|Akihabara]].
The shrine also anchors the district's festival calendar; [[mayuri|
Mayuri]] has helped with the summer festival stall every year since she
was nine.

::section[Assessment]{icon="🧪"}

The wiki's editors flag Luka as the cast's best answer to a common
misreading of the show — that the D-Mails are about wish fulfillment. Every
sender learns the same lesson at different prices: ==the message changes
the world, not the sender's standing in it==. Luka's page documents the
highest price paid for that lesson, and the most grace shown in paying it.

- Shrine duties: sweeping, wardings, and guarding a storeroom whose
  inventory sheet has been wrong since 2005.
- See [[wp:Miko]] for the tradition Luka trains in.
- Character-song discography is tracked at [[luka-discography]]. #stub

[^relic]: How a SERN-critical vintage computer ends up as a shrine offering
    is answered, hilariously and then chillingly, across [[episode-10]] and
    the [[alpha-worldline|Alpha]] finale.

Maho Hiyajo is a senior researcher at [[viktor-chondria-university|Viktor
Chondria University]], co-creator of the [[amadeus-system|Amadeus]]
memory-model AI, and the person who knew [[kurisu|Kurisu Makise]] best in
the years America had her. On the [[beta-worldline|Beta worldline]] she
arrives in Japan carrying two things: the Amadeus build containing her
dead friend's memories, and a grief she has decided to call a research
program.

::section[Salieri]{icon="🎹"}

Maho's self-mythology runs through [[wp:Antonio Salieri]] — the capable
musician history remembers mostly for standing next to Mozart. She was
Kurisu's *senpai*: older, earlier into the program, and then, permanently,
second. The show treats her framing with more respect than she treats
herself; the text is clear that ==Amadeus exists because Salieri built
it==, and that Kurisu knew exactly which of them could.[^salieri]

:::tip
Watch her hands, not her dialogue. Maho states her positions calmly and
then plays piano like she is trying to break it. The animators used the
piano as her polygraph.
:::

::section[In Akihabara]{icon="🗼"}

:::figure{align="right" width="270"}
![VCU delegation at the lab](https://picsum.photos/seed/maho-lab/270/170 "The VCU delegation visits the Future Gadget Lab, December 2010.")
:::

Sent to Japan for the Amadeus lecture circuit alongside
[[alexis-leskinen|Professor Leskinen]], Maho collides with the
[[future-gadget-laboratory|Future Gadget Laboratory]] and with
[[okabe|Okabe]] — the one person whose grief for Kurisu matches hers and
whose reasons cannot be spoken aloud. Their wary alliance becomes the
emotional spine of the Beta arc: two executors of the same estate,
comparing inventories.

She is also, notably, the first outsider to reconstruct the truth of the
[[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]] from evidence alone — Kurisu's
surviving files, plus the lab's conspicuous silences.[^recon]

::section[Across the worldlines]{icon="🌐"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Beta"}
Central. She guards the Amadeus data through the
[[strategic-focus-lab|SFL]] betrayal, burns what has to burn, and earns a
place on the short list of people Okabe trusts with worldline truth.
:::
:::tab{label="Steins;Gate"}
A visiting researcher who strikes up an unlikely friendship with a
Japanese undergraduate she has technically never met. Some connections
appear to be [[worldline-attractor-theory|attractor-stable]]. #lore
:::
::::

::section[Amadeus access log]{icon="🔐"}

A partial SFL audit log, recovered during the Beta arc's endgame, records
who actually talked to the Kurisu instance and how often. The wiki
reproduces the non-classified rows because the sorted table tells the
whole story by itself:

| User | Sessions | Total hours |
|---|---|---|
| M. Hiyajo | 312 | 208.5 |
| R. Okabe | 88 | 141.2 |
| A. Leskinen | 41 | 12.0 |
| SFL staff (aggregate) | 133 | 36.4 |

Leskinen built it and barely spoke to it. The two grieving people could
not stop. Sort by hours-per-session for the bleakest column in the
franchise.

::section[Trivia]{icon="✨"}

- Her Amadeus access phrase is a Mozart Köchel number; [[daru|Daru]]
  guessed it in four tries and has never let her forget it.
- Carries Kurisu's actual research notebook — paper, water-stained —

:::

Moeka Kiryu is a pale, silent woman who [[okabe|Okabe]] first encounters in
[[akihabara|Akihabara]] while she is hunting for a retro computer — the same
IBN 5100 the lab needs to decode [[sern|SERN's]] internal reports. She types
constantly, answers questions by holding her phone screen up to your face,
and joins the [[future-gadget-laboratory|Future Gadget Laboratory]] as Lab
Member No. 005 with a smile that never once reaches her eyes.

She is also, on the [[alpha-worldline|Alpha worldline]], the field leader of
the [[rounders|Rounders]] unit that raids the lab in [[episode-12]] — the
event that turns the story from comedy into tragedy and sets [[okabe|Okabe]]
on his long war against causality.

::section[The phone]{icon="📱"}

:::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
::::column
Moeka's phone is the entire architecture of her personality. Her handler —
known to her only as **FB** — communicates exclusively through it, and years
of that arrangement have hollowed out every other relationship she has.
When she loses access to FB in one worldline, the collapse that follows is
total: not grief exactly, but the removal of the only load-bearing wall in
a person.

Lab records credit her with the fastest confirmed typing speed of any
member — [[daru|Daru]] clocked her at ==120 words per minute on a numeric
keypad== before she noticed him counting and left the room.
::::
::::column
:::danger
On Alpha-line branches, do not mistake her silence for passivity. The raid
of August 2010 was planned around the lab's own schedule, which means she
had been reporting on it for weeks — as a member.
:::
::::
:::::

::section[History]{icon="📜"}

Little of Moeka's background survives in any verifiable form; the following
is assembled from Rounders personnel fragments recovered by [[daru|Daru]]
and from her own sparse statements. She grew up effectively invisible —
the kind of person teachers forgot to call on — and was recruited into
SERN's [[rounders|Rounders]] program in her late teens, apparently selected
*because* nobody would miss her.[^recruit] FB gave her a codename, a
mission, and a reason to wake up, in that order of importance.

| Period | Known activity |
|---|---|
| ~2005 | First contact with the recruiter later identified as FB |
| 2008 | Formal Rounders induction, codename M4 |
| 2009 | Deep-cover placement as freelance editor |
| 2010-07 | Tasked with locating the IBN 5100 |
| 2010-08 | Joins the lab; leads the raid days later ([[alpha-worldline|Alpha]]) |
| 2010-08 | Neutralized during [[okabe|Okabe's]] D-Mail counter-operations |

::section[Across the worldlines]{icon="🌐"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Alpha"}
The loyal instrument. She executes the raid, reports the lab's
[[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]] to SERN, and is discarded by her
employers almost immediately afterward — a detail Okabe only appreciates
much later.
:::
:::tab{label="Beta"}
On [[beta-worldline|Beta]] branches she never receives the order. She
drifts through Akihabara still hunting the IBN 5100 for a handler who has
stopped answering, which may be the crueler fate.
:::
:::tab{label="Steins;Gate"}
A freelance editor with a bad phone habit and no handler at all. She still
doesn't talk much. Some architecture doesn't rebuild just because the war
that built it never happened.
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="Spoilers: the identity of FB"}
FB is [[yuugo-tennouji|Yuugo Tennouji]] — Mr. Braun, the lab's own
landlord, himself a Rounder pressed into service years earlier. The
revelation lands twice: once for the betrayal, and once for the symmetry,
because FB ran Moeka exactly the way SERN ran him — through the one channel
of affection the target could not afford to lose. The name comes from
*Ferdinand Braun*, inventor of the CRT.[^fb]
:::

::section[Assessment]{icon="🧪"}

:::warning
Lab members reviewing this page after a worldline shift should re-verify
every field in the infobox against their own [[divergence-meter|Reading
Steiner]] recollection. Moeka's records are the least stable of any member;
RS-corroborated details are marked in the edit history. #lore
:::

Her SOC service file — three pages, mostly redacted — was recovered from a
SERN mirror by [[daru|Daru]] during [[operation-verdandi]]. It lists a
psychological profile in exactly four words: *"Loyal to the channel."*

::section[See also]{icon="🔗"}

- [[rounders|The Rounders]] — the unit she leads on Alpha branches
- [[yuugo-tennouji|Yuugo Tennouji]] — her handler, and the page's biggest spoiler
- [[episode-12]] — the raid
- [[wp:Parasocial interaction]] — the real-world psychology her FB
  dependency dramatizes

[^recruit]: The recruitment fragment is authenticity-disputed; it surfaced
    on [[atchannel|@channel]] before Daru's crawl found the original.
[^fb]: Karl Ferdinand Braun shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics. The
    codename is either an electronics-history joke or a coincidence SERN's
    SOC never bothered to correct.

Nae Tennouji is the young daughter of [[yuugo-tennouji|Mr. Braun]], raised
in the CRT shop under the [[future-gadget-lab|Future Gadget Lab]] and
functionally adopted as the building's little sister. She trails after
[[mayuri|Mayuri]], tolerates [[okabe|Okabe's]] theatrics with a
politeness beyond her years, and sees — because children in shops see
everything — considerably more of the building's secrets than anyone
credits.

::section[What Nae knows]{icon="👀"}

:::note
This section is deliberately understated in the anime and easy to miss.
Nae is present, in the background, for at least three scenes where FB's
phone is in frame. The wiki takes no position on what an eleven-year-old
made of it. The [[alpha-worldline|Alpha]] visual-novel route takes one.
:::

:::collapse{title="Spoilers: the Alpha route's darkest branch"}
One infamous Alpha branch follows Nae after she pieces together her
father's double life and its ending. The branch fast-forwards fifteen
years to a Nae who has joined the [[rounders|Rounders]] herself — not out
of loyalty to SERN but to get close enough to the people who used her
father to return the favor. It is the franchise's bleakest ending, and the
strongest argument in the text that ==the Rounders system is
self-perpetuating by design==: it manufactures the orphans it later
recruits. #lore
:::

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Alpha"}
A child in a building full of secrets, orbiting a tragedy she cannot see
the shape of yet. In the worst branch (above), its inheritor.
:::
:::tab{label="Beta"}
Simply a kid: homework at the shop counter, crane games with Mayuri on
Sundays, a father who is only a shopkeeper. What the lab is fighting for,
in miniature.
:::
:::tab{label="Steins;Gate"}
As Beta, plus one strange grown-up part-timer on a bicycle whom she
adores without ever learning is family — her niece, born decades from

::section[Life in the building]{icon="🏢"}

:::::columns{ratio="55-45"}

The Tennouji apartment, [[braun-tsuushin|the shop]], and the

building itself: the [[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]] tripping the
