Shouichi Makise, publishing in disgrace under the alias **Nakabachi**, is a
failed theoretical physicist, the father of [[kurisu|Kurisu Makise]], and —
on the [[beta-worldline|Beta worldline]] — the man whose stolen conference
papers ignite World War III. He is the story's only true villain in the
domestic sense of the word: SERN is an institution, but Nakabachi is just a
man who could not forgive his own daughter for surpassing him.

::section[The fall]{icon="📉"}

His early career was genuinely distinguished — his mid-90s work on closed
timelike curves is still cited, and taught Kurisu her first physics at the
dinner table.[^dinner] The decline began when the field moved past him and
his daughter did not stop moving with it. By 2003 he had been dismissed
from his university post; by 2010 the alias, the debts, and the venue-rate
conference bookings had consumed what remained of the name Makise.

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1992 | Marries; Kurisu born the following year |
| 1996 | Publishes his highest-cited paper |
| 2001 | First public priority dispute — against a 8-year-old Kurisu's notebook, per family accounts |
| 2003 | Dismissed from Tokyo Denki University |
| 2005 | Adopts the Nakabachi alias; family separates |
| 2010-07-28 | The [[radio-kaikan\|Radio Kaikan]] conference ([[episode-01]]) |
| 2010-11 | Defects with the stolen thesis ([[beta-worldline\|Beta]]) |

::section[July 28]{icon="🗓️"}

:::danger
This section spoils the opening *and* the ending of the entire series. The
same afternoon, in the same building, is the story's first scene and its
last battlefield. Proceed accordingly, or begin with [[episode-01]].
:::

:::collapse{title="Spoilers: what happens in that room"}
On Beta-line branches, the argument in the Radio Kaikan ends with Kurisu
bleeding out on the eighth floor — the body [[okabe|Okabe]] finds in the
story's opening minutes. Nakabachi flees with her time-travel thesis to
sell abroad; the paper's contents, developed by a state program over the
following decades, produce the war that [[suzuha-amane|Suzuha's]] future is
fleeing. Every attempt Okabe makes to save Kurisu without addressing the
*paper* fails: the [[steins-gate-worldline|Steins Gate]] solution finally
threads the needle by ensuring the thesis burns while the world — and
Nakabachi himself — believes his daughter died anyway. Operation Skuld's
cruelest requirement is that ==the lie must include the liar==.
:::

::section[The authorship question]{icon="⚖️"}

:::::columns{ratio="55-45"}
::::column
The thesis Nakabachi carries out of the Radio Kaikan is Kurisu's work —
written in her notation, on her problem, extending *her* [[time-leap-machine|
time-leap]] results. His marginal annotations, recovered on one branch,
amount to renaming variables. The wiki records the paper under her
authorship and files his claim where it belongs: in the long, sour
tradition catalogued at [[wp:List of scientific priority disputes]].
::::
::::column
:::warning
Fandom shorthand calls him "Doctor Nakabachi," but no institution on any
worldline has ever verified the doctorate post-2003. The title is part of
the alias. #lore
:::
::::
:::::

::section[Whereabouts by worldline]{icon="🌐"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Alpha"}
A minor embarrassment on the conference circuit. With [[sern|SERN]]
monopolizing time-travel research, his stolen-thesis gambit has no buyer,
and Alpha branches simply forget him — the fate he feared more than any
prison.
:::
:::tab{label="Beta"}
The war's accidental author. Defects via a Russian intermediary in
November 2010; last confirmed sighting is an airport camera frame that
[[daru|Daru]] pulls in [[episode-23]].
:::
:::tab{label="Steins;Gate"}
The thesis burns in the Radio Kaikan with the world watching a different
story. He leaves the building with an empty envelope and a live daughter,
convinced of the opposite on both counts.
:::
::::

::section[Assessment]{icon="🧪"}

What makes Nakabachi durable as a villain is his scale. He has no
organization, no [[committee-of-300|Committee]], no ideology — only a
wounded vanity with a twenty-year head start. SERN needed a global
conspiracy to nearly end the world; he nearly ends it with a manila
envelope. The contrast is the point, and the reason his page sits here
among People rather than beside [[sern|SERN]] in
[[Organizations|Category: Organizations]].

[^dinner]: Kurisu's own account, related in [[episode-22]]: the last time
    physics was something they did *together* she was seven. She kept the
    notebook.

# Suzuha Amane

:::infobox{title="Suzuha Amane" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/suzuha-amane/300/180" caption="Lab Member No. 004, on loan from 2036."}

Suzuha Amane is a time traveler from the year 2036, sent to the present by a
resistance cell fighting a global order enforced by [[sern|SERN]]. She spends
most of 2010 undercover as a part-time clerk at Braun Tsuushin, the
CRT-repair shop run by an old man she knows only as her employer — and who
is, unbeknownst to either of them for most of the story, her own father,
[[yuugo-tennouji|Yuugo Tennouji]].

She later joins the [[future-gadget-laboratory|Future Gadget Laboratory]] as
Lab Member No. 004, bringing a soldier's directness that clashes, then
gels, with [[okabe|Okabe]]'s theatrics. Her mission is simple to state and
brutal to execute: stop the timeline that produces the world she was born
into — a world under martial rule, its populace surveilled through
technology descended from Future Gadget Lab research that SERN captured
and weaponized.

::section[Mission]{icon="🎯"}

:::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
::::column
Suzuha's future is one where SERN, having perfected time travel decades
ahead of anyone else, used that head start to consolidate total control.
Her cell's plan hinges on preventing SERN from ever recovering the
[[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]]'s underlying research — which means
staying close to the one lab reckless enough to keep reinventing it. She
carries a time machine capable of one-way jumps into the past; getting home
again is a separate, much harder problem she does not discuss with the lab
until she has to.

Her public cover story borrows the name **John Titor** — a nod to an old
internet legend about a soldier from 2036 who claimed to have traveled back
looking for an IBN 5100-class computer.[^titor] Lab members who catch the
reference never quite believe the coincidence is a coincidence.
::::
::::column
:::note
Suzuha never volunteers her real objective outright. Most of what the lab
learns about 2036 comes out sideways, in offhand remarks she immediately
tries to walk back.
:::

:::tip
Her bicycle isn't decoration — in at least one worldline it's how she wins
a race against a car through central [[akihabara|Akihabara]], and how she
buys Okabe the seconds he needs at the climax of the July incident.
:::
::::
:::::

::section[Personality]{icon="🎭"}

Blunt, athletic, and allergic to Okabe's mad-scientist routine — at least
at first. She calls him "Okarin" only once she's stopped pretending she
finds him ridiculous. Underneath the deadpan is someone carrying a
==decades-heavy== sense of duty: she was raised, in effect, by a cause, and
it shows in how quickly she reverts to soldier-mode the moment a plan is
threatened. She's fiercely protective of [[mayuri|Mayuri]] and unexpectedly
gentle with [[nae-tennouji|Nae Tennouji]], the granddaughter of the man she
doesn't yet know is her father.

:::collapse{title="Spoilers: what she learns about her father"}
Late in the story, when the lab pieces together Mr. Braun's history —
a granddaughter lost to illness, a shop kept running out of stubbornness
more than income — Suzuha realizes the timeline math lines up with her own
birth record. She chooses not to tell him. What she gets from the arc
instead is quieter: proof that the version of him she grew up idolizing
second-hand was, in fact, exactly that ordinary and exactly that brave.
:::

::section[Role across worldlines]{icon="🌐"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Alpha"}
On [[alpha-worldline|Alpha]] branches, Suzuha's mission mostly fails —
SERN's grip tightens regardless of what the lab does, and she's forced to
consider more drastic interventions.
:::
:::tab{label="Beta"}
On [[beta-worldline|Beta]] branches, the timeline diverges hard enough
that SERN's future never quite forms the way she remembers it, which is
either good news or a sign she's already changed more than she meant to.
:::
:::tab{label="Steins;Gate"}
On the [[steins-gate-worldline|Steins Gate]] line, her mission and Okabe's
finally point the same direction, and for once neither of them has to lie
to the other about the stakes.
:::
::::

Yuugo Tennouji — universally "Mr. Braun," after the [[wp:Karl Ferdinand
Braun|inventor of the CRT]] he refuses to stop selling — is the landlord of
the building that houses the [[future-gadget-lab|Future Gadget Lab]], a
single father to [[nae-tennouji|Nae]], and the loudest fixture of the
[[akihabara|Akihabara]] backstreet the lab calls home. He bellows at
[[okabe|Okabe]] about the rent, the noise, and the microwave that keeps
browning out his shop's power, roughly in that order, roughly daily.

On the [[alpha-worldline|Alpha worldline]] he is also **FB** — the
[[rounders|Rounders]] handler who has been running [[moeka-kiryu|Moeka
Kiryu]] for years from the floor directly beneath the lab he was assigned
to watch.

::section[The shopkeeper]{icon="🏪"}

:::figure{align="right" width="280"}
![Braun Tsuushin storefront](https://picsum.photos/seed/braun-shop/280/180 "The shop: forty CRTs, zero flatscreens, one enormous opinion.")
:::

[[braun-tsuushin|Braun Tsuushin]] sells and repairs cathode-ray tube
televisions exclusively, a business model that stopped making sense around
2003 and that Tennouji defends with the zeal of a man who is either a
romantic or laundering something.[^shop] The truth is a little of both:
the shop is real, the love of the technology is real, and the shop is
*also* how SERN pays him.

He took the work for one reason. Nae's medical bills after her mother's
death would have ended the shop, and SERN's recruiter — as SERN's
recruiters reliably do — arrived within a week of the funeral with exactly
the right number on a piece of paper.

::section[FB]{icon="🕶️"}

:::danger
Everything below the fold here is an Alpha-line spoiler, and it is the big
one for this character. See [[episode-19]] before reading.
:::

:::collapse{title="Spoilers: the handler beneath the floorboards"}
As FB, Tennouji ran Moeka through text messages composed on an old phone
he kept taped under the shop counter — close enough to the lab's
[[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]] that at least one D-Mail is believed
to have shifted a worldline while sitting in his outbox. He never met her
face to face until the day the arrangement collapsed, and by every
recovered account he had come to think of her, with genuine and useless
tenderness, as a second daughter.

When SERN ordered him to cut her loose, he obeyed — the same way he had
obeyed for eleven years, because obedience was the price of Nae's future.
The scene where Okabe confronts him is played almost without anger: two
men who both know exactly what SERN costs, itemized.
:::

The Suzuha connection means Tennouji's bloodline is load-bearing for the
entire [[steins-gate-worldline|Steins Gate]] endgame — a fact precisely

His genetics gave Suzuha the frame that survives a one-way trip through

open?" — turns out to be load-bearing foreshadowing. [[daru|Daru's]]

# Attractor Field Theory

:::infobox{title="Attractor Field Theory" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/attractor/300/180" caption="All rivers in a valley reach the same sea."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Type | Theoretical framework |
| Domain | Worldline dynamics |
| Key claim | Worldlines cluster into fields converging on fixed events |
| Named fields | [[alpha-worldline\|Alpha]], [[beta-worldline\|Beta]], others conjectured |
| Boundary indicator | Integer part of divergence value |
| Escape mechanism | Divergence beyond field boundary |
| Anomalous region | [[steins-gate-worldline\|Steins Gate]] (≈1.048596) |
| Instrument | [[divergence-meter\|Divergence Meter]] |
| Status within lab | Working model; predictive record strong |
:::

**Attractor Field Theory** is the [[future-gadget-lab|lab]]'s working
model of how worldlines behave under interference. Its core claim: history
is not one thread but a bundle, and the bundle is *combed*. Individual
worldlines within a field may differ in any amount of detail — who won a
bar quiz, whether a computer was donated to a shrine — but all of them
bend toward the same **convergence events**, which occur in every
worldline of the field regardless of intervention. Change the path all you
like; the destination holds.

The theory is why the lab's early optimism about D-Mails curdled. Undoing
a *cause* does not undo a *converged effect* — the field simply reroutes,
and the rerouting is not gentle. #lore

::section[Structure of a field]{icon="🕸️"}

::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
:::column
Worldlines are indexed by **divergence**, the number the
[[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]] displays. The integer part names
the field: readings in `0.x` belong to the Alpha field, `1.x` to Beta.
Within a field, the fractional digits measure how far a worldline sits
from the field's central "channel" — but ==distance within a field buys
detail, not destiny==. An Alpha worldline at 0.33 and one at 0.57 disagree
about months of events and agree perfectly about the ones that matter.

Crossing *between* fields requires pushing divergence across the integer
boundary — an intervention so structurally large that the entire causal
chain feeding a convergence event fails at once. The lab has achieved this
exactly twice, in both directions, and neither method is recommended
reading before bed. See [[episode-13|Episode 13]] and
[[episode-16|Episode 16]].
:::
:::column
**Known convergence events**

- Alpha: a death in the lab's first
  summer; SERN's future
  dominion — see
  [[alpha-worldline#convergence]]
- Beta: a different death;
  a war over time travel —
  see [[beta-worldline#convergence]]
- Steins Gate: ==none known==
:::
::::

```mermaid
graph TD;
AlphaField-->ConvergenceA;
BetaField-->ConvergenceB;
AlphaField-->SteinsGate;
SteinsGate-->NoConvergence;
```

::section[The river metaphor]{icon="🏞️"}

The lab's standard explanation, owed to the future visitor who delivered
the meter: a field is a valley, worldlines are rivers, convergence events
are the sea. Rain falling anywhere in the valley reaches the same sea; to
reach a *different* sea you must leave the valley, and valleys are
separated by watersheds — high, hostile, and narrow. The Steins Gate
worldline, in this metaphor, is a river that ==exits through a cave no map
shows== and empties somewhere no one has charted. The metaphor is
acknowledged to break down exactly here, which lab consensus holds is the
metaphor working as intended.

::section[Predictions and record]{icon="📈"}

| Prediction | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Undo mail cannot restore exact prior reading | 3 undo mails | Confirmed — residuals of 10⁻⁶ every time |
| Convergence event recurs despite cause removal | 5 interventions | Confirmed, 5/5, at rising personal cost |
| Time leaps cannot change fields | 6 leaps | Confirmed — intra-field motion only |
| Field boundary requires causal-chain collapse | 2 crossings | Confirmed |
| Omega field exists above 3.0 | 1 anomalous reading | Unconfirmed #stub |

:::warning
The theory's confirmed predictions are all *negative* — it tells you what
cannot work. The lab treats any plan that "just needs the attractor field
to make an exception" as automatically failed. This is written on the
whiteboard in the ink that doesn't erase.
:::

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Strong reading"}
Convergence is ontological: the field enforces its events the way geometry
enforces triangle angles. Interventions don't *fight* the field; they were
always part of it. Favored by [[kurisu|Kurisu]] on odd-numbered days.
:::
:::tab{label="Weak reading"}
Convergence is statistical: enough causal mass accumulates around certain
events that removing any one cause leaves thousands. Escape isn't
forbidden, merely astronomically unlikely — which is why it took a
[[time-leap-machine|leap machine]], eleven attempts, and a deception
operation to manage it once. Favored by Kurisu on even-numbered days.
:::
:::tab{label="Okabe reading"}
"The field is the will of Steins Gate, and it can be *negotiated with*."
Not a theory by any formal standard; predictive record, embarrassingly,
also 5/5.
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="Relation to established physics"}
The theory freeloads on the [[wp:Many-worlds interpretation]] for its
plurality of histories and on dynamical-systems language
([[wp:Attractor]]) for its central image, while being rigorously faithful
to neither. Kurisu's notebook files it under "phenomenology that works,"
the drawer above "physics," with a cross-reference reading: *a model that
predicts eleven for eleven has earned the right to be wrong later.*
:::

::section[See also]{icon="🔗"}

# D-Mail

:::infobox{title="D-Mail" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/dmail/300/180" caption="Subject: (no subject). Delivered: yesterday."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Full name | De Lorean Mail |
| Coined by | [[okabe\|Rintaro Okabe]] |
| Medium | SMS text message |
| Transmitter | [[phone-microwave\|Phone Microwave]] |
| Payload limit | 36 bytes per burst (12–18 characters Japanese) |
| Direction | Present → past only |
| Observable effect | Worldline shift at moment of receipt |
| Detection | SERN monitoring network |
| Countermeasure | Sending a cancelling D-Mail ("undo mail") |
| Total confirmed sends | 11 (this attractor field) |
| Status | Retired practice |
:::

A **D-Mail** (De Lorean Mail — [[okabe|Okabe]] does not apologize for the
name) is a text message transmitted into the past via the
[[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]]. It is the lab's founding discovery,
the trigger for every worldline shift in the lab's recorded history, and
the reason this wiki's event pages must all be annotated with divergence
values. As lab doctrine now states, in letters large enough to read from
the doorway: ==a D-Mail cannot be unsent, only outbid==.

::section[Properties]{icon="📜"}

::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
:::column
A D-Mail arrives on a real handset in the past as an ordinary message —
no glow, no fanfare, sender field garbled. The recipient acts on it (or
doesn't), causality re-knits around the new information, and the worldline
shifts to accommodate the changed history. From inside the new worldline,
the message has "always" been received; only observers with Reading
Steiner recall the version of events it overwrote.

Payload capacity is the binding constraint. The PhoneWave's aperture
stays open for microseconds, enough for roughly **36 bytes** per burst.
Longer messages fragment into multiple bursts that can arrive out of
order, minutes apart — the lab's second D-Mail arrived as three fragments
across two hours, and the recipient read them in exactly the wrong
order.[^1]
:::
:::column
**Anatomy of a send**

1. Compose SMS on docked handset
2. Set target time offset
3. Microwave runs (do not open)
4. Message ceases to exist *here*
5. World quietly rewrites itself
:::
::::

::section[Rules of thumb]{icon="📏"}

The lab's accumulated, expensively-learned guidance:

| Rule | Reason | Learned in |
|---|---|---|
| Never send about money | Divergence explodes; SERN flags gambling anomalies | [[episode-05\|Episode 05]] |
| Never send about people's lives | The attractor field routes around it, cruelly | [[episode-12\|Episode 12]] |
| Shorter is safer | Fragmentation scrambles meaning | [[episode-03\|Episode 03]] |
| Photograph the [[divergence-meter\|meter]] first | Only way to measure what you did | [[episode-06\|Episode 06]] |
| The undo mail must contradict, not delete | The past cannot un-know; it can only be re-persuaded | [[episode-13\|Episode 13]] |

:::tip
An "undo mail" does not restore the original worldline — it moves to a
*third* worldline that closely resembles the first. The
[[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]] readings before and after an undo
never match exactly. The difference has never been observed to be zero.
:::

::section[Notable D-Mails]{icon="📮"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="The first"}
A one-line test message. It arrived one week in the past, and the shift it
caused was large enough that the lab's founding membership *changed* —
the canonical example of how disproportionate the effect can be. Covered
in [[episode-01|Episode 01]] and [[episode-02|Episode 02]].
:::
:::tab{label="The worst"}
A lottery-number mail sent on behalf of a friend. The numbers arrived
garbled, the winnings never materialized, and the divergence cost took
three undo mails to claw back. See [[episode-10|Episode 10]].
:::
:::tab{label="The last"}
The final D-Mail sent from the lab was an undo mail — the one that pulled
the worldline out of the [[alpha-worldline|Alpha attractor field]]
entirely. Its 12 characters are redacted on this wiki by unanimous lab
vote. [[episode-13|Episode 13]].
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="Why 'De Lorean'?"}
Okabe named it after the time-travelling car from a film he claims to have
watched "for research." Attempts to rename it ("Retro-SMS," "chronomail,"
Daru's unprintable suggestion) all failed to stick. The abbreviations table
on this wiki lists D-Mail as canonical, so the argument is officially
over.
:::

::section[Detection and interception]{icon="🛰️"}

Every D-Mail transits the public cellular network for the mundane half of
its journey, which is how SERN's monitoring net caught the lab so quickly
— the temporal burst is exotic, but the SMS itself is just an SMS. Later
sends were routed through a chain of anonymizing relays Daru assembled,
which bought weeks at most. The uncomfortable lesson, recorded in the
[[lab-member-handbook|handbook]]: *information that changes the past is
still information, and information leaks.* For the theoretical framing of
why worldlines converge despite interference, see
[[attractor-field|Attractor field theory]] and the overview at
[[wp:Many-worlds interpretation]].

![Send log](https://picsum.photos/seed/dmail-log/420/200 "The lab's手書き send log. Entries 7 through 9 are taped over.")
:::

[^1]: The resulting misunderstanding is commemorated by a small dent in
    the lab's refrigerator door.

# Divergence Meter

:::infobox{title="Divergence Meter" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/divmeter/300/180" caption="1.048596 — the number everyone is chasing."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Designation | Divergence Meter (no FG number assigned) |
| Function | Displays the current worldline's divergence value |
| Display | Eight Nixie tubes, seven significant digits |
| Origin | Delivered to the lab by a future visitor |
| Readable by | Anyone; *interpretable* only with Reading Steiner |
| Reference values | Alpha < 1%, Beta ≥ 1%, Steins Gate ≈ 1.048596 |
| Power draw | ~12 W continuous |
| Housed at | [[future-gadget-lab\|Future Gadget Laboratory]] |
| Maintained by | [[okabe\|Rintaro Okabe]] |
| Replication status | One working replica, built decades early |
| Status | Operational |
:::

The **Divergence Meter** is a Nixie-tube instrument that displays a single
number: the **divergence value** of the worldline the observer currently
occupies, measured against an arbitrary zero point. It is the only
instrument the [[future-gadget-lab|Future Gadget Laboratory]] possesses that
can distinguish one worldline from another from the *inside* — without it,
a shift caused by a D-Mail is detectable only by people whose memories
survive the transition.

Unlike the [[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]] and the
[[time-leap-machine|Time Leap Machine]], the meter was not invented at the
lab — at least, not yet. The unit on the lab's workbench was ==delivered by
a visitor who claimed to come from decades in the future==, along with the
schematics needed to eventually build it. The lab therefore maintains the
awkward position of owning a device it will not invent for another
thirty-odd years. #lore

::section[Reading the meter]{icon="👁️"}

::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
:::column
The display shows a fixed-point decimal such as `1.048596`. The integer
part identifies the **attractor field** — the broad basin of worldlines
that converge toward the same major events — and the fractional digits
identify the specific worldline within it. Values below 1.000000 belong to
the [[alpha-worldline|Alpha attractor field]]; values from 1.000000 up
(excluding the anomalous Steins Gate band) belong to
[[beta-worldline|Beta]].

Crucially, the meter's reading changes *at the instant* of a worldline
shift, but only an observer with Reading Steiner will notice, because for
everyone else the meter has "always" shown the new value. Okabe's habit of
photographing the display before every experiment exists precisely to
defeat this: the photo changes too, but his memory of taking it doesn't.
:::
:::column
**Reference readings**

- `0.337187` — deep Alpha
- `0.571024` — Alpha, late-stage
- `1.048596` — ==Steins Gate==
- `1.130205` — Beta
- `3.406288` — unconfirmed #stub
:::
::::

::section[Recorded values]{icon="📊"}

A sortable log of readings photographed at the lab. Compare with the
episode-by-episode account in the [[episode-guide]].

| Reading | Attractor field | Context | First noted |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.337187 | Alpha | Deepest recorded Alpha excursion | [[episode-12\|Episode 12]] |
| 0.409431 | Alpha | After the lottery D-Mail was undone | [[episode-10\|Episode 10]] |
| 0.456903 | Alpha | Baseline for mid-series experiments | [[episode-06\|Episode 06]] |
| 0.523299 | Alpha | Post-IBN retrieval | [[episode-09\|Episode 09]] |
| 0.571024 | Alpha | Final Alpha reading | [[episode-13\|Episode 13]] |
| 1.048596 | Steins Gate | Target value | [[episode-16\|Episode 16]] |
| 1.064750 | Beta | First Beta confirmation | [[episode-14\|Episode 14]] |
| 1.130205 | Beta | Stable Beta plateau | [[episode-15\|Episode 15]] |

:::note
The meter does not *predict*. A reading of `1.048596` does not mean events
will go well; it means the worldline is outside both the Alpha and Beta
attractor fields' convergence — free, for better or worse, of their fixed
outcomes. See [[steins-gate-worldline]].
:::

::section[Construction]{icon="🔧"}

The replica was built by [[okabe|Okabe]] and [[daru|Daru]] from the
future schematics, sourcing IN-14 Nixie tubes from a stall in
[[akihabara|Akihabara]]'s back streets and a driver board hand-etched at
the lab. Each tube requires roughly 170 V to strike; the boost converter's
output capacitor stores

$$E = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(47\,\mu F)(170\,\text{V})^2 \approx 0.68\ \text{J}$$

which is trivial next to the PhoneWave's discharge but enough to bite a
careless finger.[^1] The sensing element — the part that actually measures
divergence — is not documented in the schematics at all. The delivered unit
contains a sealed module the lab has never opened, on the visitor's advice
that ==opening it voids more than the warranty==.

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Display board"}
Eight IN-14 tubes, multiplexed 4:1. Daru's firmware refreshes at 120 Hz to
kill visible flicker on camera — important, given how often the thing gets
photographed.
:::
:::tab{label="Sensor module"}
Sealed. Mass 412 g, faintly warm, no external connections besides power and
a one-wire data line. The lab's collective decision is to not think about
it too hard.
:::
:::tab{label="Enclosure"}
Walnut and brushed aluminum, machined at the
[[braun-tube-workshop|Braun Tube Workshop]] downstairs in exchange for a
month of shop-sitting.
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="The future visitor (spoilers)"}
The person who delivered the meter also delivered a warning about what the
Alpha attractor field converges *to*. Their identity is discussed on the
worldline pages rather than here; suffice to say the lab had a personal
stake in believing them. See [[alpha-worldline#convergence]] for the
long-run outcome the meter helped everyone escape.
:::

::section[See also]{icon="🔗"}

:::figure{align="right" width="250"}
![Nixie tubes](https://picsum.photos/seed/nixie/250/160 "IN-14 tubes mid-multiplex. The camera catches what the eye can't.")
:::

For the physics-adjacent background on cold-cathode displays, see
[[wp:Nixie tube]]. The meter's readings anchor the timeline notation used
across this wiki — every event page cites a divergence value where one is
known. Related: [[attractor-field|Attractor field theory]],
[[d-mail|D-Mail]], and the never-built
[[divergence-meter-mk2|pocket divergence meter]] Daru keeps proposing.

[^1]: Twice. Both times Daru, both times the same finger.

# Future Gadget #1: Bit Particle Cannon

:::infobox{title="FG #1 — Bit Particle Cannon" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/fg01/300/180" caption="It is a TV remote. It is ALSO a particle cannon."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Designation | Future Gadget #1 |
| Common name | Bit Particle Cannon |
| Actual function | Universal infrared remote control |
| Claimed function | Directed-energy weapon (aspirational) |
| Inventor | [[okabe\|Rintaro Okabe]] |
| Range | ~8 m line-of-sight |
| Power source | Two AA batteries |
| Mass | 340 g (mostly decorative heatsink) |
| Notable use | Turning off every CRT in the [[braun-tube-workshop\|Braun Tube Workshop]] at once |
| Status | Functional |
:::

**Future Gadget #1**, the **Bit Particle Cannon**, is the founding entry in
the [[future-gadget-lab|Future Gadget Laboratory]]'s product line and the
purest expression of the lab's design philosophy: take something mundane,
give it a name that implies war crimes, and refuse to acknowledge the gap.
Functionally, it is a high-gain universal infrared remote control shaped
like a raygun. [[okabe|Okabe]] maintains that infrared photons are
particles and that the device fires them in bits; therefore, *Bit Particle
Cannon*. The logic is airtight and everyone hates it.

::section[Design]{icon="🔧"}

::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
:::column
The Cannon's emitter stage gangs twelve IR LEDs behind a salvaged camera
lens, giving it roughly four times the effective range of a consumer
remote and a beam tight enough to switch off one specific television
across a store floor without touching its neighbors. The trigger maps to a
learning chip that can store 64 device codes; a thumb dial on the "power
regulator" (a repurposed volume knob) selects among them.

The distinctive silhouette — fins, vents, an entirely non-functional
charging coil — was vacuum-formed by [[daru|Daru]] from a model kit and
sprayed lab-signature silver. The heatsink dissipates no heat. It has
never needed to. It stays.
:::
:::column
**Stored device codes (excerpt)**

- Lab CRT (main)
- Lab air conditioner #wip
- Every TV, [[braun-tube-workshop|downstairs]]
- The [[may-queen-nyan-nyan|May Queen]] menu display (by request, once)
:::
::::

::section[Operational history]{icon="📜"}

| Incident | Target | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| First firing | Lab television | Success; channel changed from 6 m |
| The Braun affair | 22 CRTs simultaneously | Success; ban from shop floor, since lifted |
| [[episode-02\|Episode 02]] demonstration | [[kurisu\|Kurisu]]'s patience | Failure |
| Comima booth demo | Crowd of 40 | Partial success; three sales |
| Blackout of 2010 | N/A | Falsely accused; alibi held |

:::note
The Cannon is the only Future Gadget ever to have *sold units* — three, at
a convention, to buyers who understood exactly what it was and wanted it
anyway. Okabe cites this as market validation. The lab's accounting
ledger, kept by [[mayuri]], records the proceeds as "snack money."
:::

::section[The physics of the bit]{icon="⚛️"}

Okabe's naming argument, reproduced here for the record: an infrared LED
emits photons of wavelength $\lambda \approx 940$ nm, each carrying energy

$$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} \approx 1.3\ \text{eV}$$

— and since the device modulates them into *bits* (the IR protocol's
on-off keying), it is, ==in the most literal sense available to physics==,
a cannon that fires particles of bits. Peer review of this argument has
been sought from exactly one qualified physicist in the lab's orbit; her
response is preserved in [[kurisu|the reviewer]]'s own words in the lab
notebook and consists of the phrase "I'm going home."

:::collapse{title="Full spec sheet"}
| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Emitter count | 12 × IR LED, 940 nm |
| Beam divergence | 3.5° |
| Modulation | NEC / RC-5 / Sony SIRC |
| Code memory | 64 slots, EEPROM |
| Trigger rating | 100,000 actuations |
| Decorative components (by mass) | 61% |
:::

::section[Legacy]{icon="🏆"}

As Future Gadget #1, the Cannon set the template every later gadget
follows: a real function, a fictional identity, and a build quality that
outlasts the joke. It predates the lab's descent into actual mad science
by over a year, and lab members are quietly protective of it for that
reason — it is the only gadget from ==before everything got complicated==.
It appears in the background of nearly every lab scene in the
[[episode-guide|episode guide]], hanging on its dedicated wall hook, next
to the fire extinguisher and the [[future-gadget-02|hooded fan]] that
became gadget #2. For the underlying consumer technology, see
[[wp:Remote control]].

# Future Gadget #2: Bamboo Helicam

:::infobox{title="FG #2 — Bamboo Helicam" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/fg02/300/180" caption="Airborne for 11 seconds. Legendary forever."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Designation | Future Gadget #2 |
| Common name | Bamboo Helicam |
| Function | Head-mounted camera drone (detachable) |
| Inventors | [[daru\|Itaru Hashida]], [[okabe\|Rintaro Okabe]] |
| Rotor | Single coaxial pair, 18 cm |
| Camera | 0.3 MP CMOS, composite out |
| Flight endurance | 11 seconds (record) |
| Control | 27 MHz AM radio, borrowed from an RC car |
| Injuries caused | 1 (minor, self-inflicted, Okabe) |
| Status | Grounded pending "rotor renaissance" |
:::

**Future Gadget #2**, the **Bamboo Helicam**, is a head-mounted detachable
camera drone: a propeller beanie that takes off. The wearer walks around
with a rotor assembly clipped to a helmet; on command, the assembly
detaches, ascends, and streams grainy video of the wearer's bald spot to a
CRT in the lab. It is the [[future-gadget-lab|lab]]'s first flying machine,
its first camera platform, and its first product recall, all within the
same week.

::section[Concept]{icon="💡"}

::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
:::column
The design brief, as written on the whiteboard and never erased: *"personal
airborne perspective at zero notice."* [[daru|Daru]] wanted an overhead
camera for crowded convention halls; [[okabe|Okabe]] wanted something that
looked like it came from a future where surveillance is whimsical. The
compromise was a coaxial rotor unit that lives on the wearer's head —
pre-positioned for launch, in the sense that a hat is pre-positioned.

The launch sequence is genuinely clever: the rotors spin up while still
clipped in, the clip releases at operating RPM, and the airframe rises
with the camera already recording. The landing sequence is the part that
was, in the language of the incident report, ==never actually designed==.
:::
:::column
**Flight log summary**

- Flight 1 — 4 s, wall
- Flight 2 — 7 s, other wall
- Flight 3 — 11 s, ceiling fan interaction
- Flight 4 — 9 s, out the window, recovered from
  [[braun-tube-workshop|Mr. Braun's]] awning
- Flight 5 — grounded by unanimous vote
:::
::::

::section[Specifications]{icon="📐"}

Sortable spec table; hover a header to sort.

| Parameter | Value | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Rotor diameter | 18 | cm |
| All-up mass | 96 | g |
| Hover power | 14 | W |
| Battery capacity | 350 | mAh |
| Theoretical endurance | 95 | s |
| Achieved endurance | 11 | s |
| Video latency | 0.4 | s |
| Cost, parts | 4,800 | ¥ |

The gap between theoretical and achieved endurance is the story of the
gadget. Hover time was never the limit — *walls* were. The 27 MHz control
link, borrowed from an RC car, has no proportional control: the rotor unit
is always either climbing at full power or falling. Daru's control law,
documented in a comment as `// good luck`, toggles between these states
several times a second, which in practice traces a flight path best
described as ==enthusiastic Brownian motion==.

:::warning
Flight 3's ceiling fan interaction embedded a rotor blade in the lab's
corkboard, 40 cm from [[mayuri|Mayuri]]'s head. FG #2 is grounded indoors
by standing order, and the corkboard hole is preserved as a safety
memorial.
:::

::section[The camera]{icon="📷"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Optics"}
A 0.3-megapixel CMOS module scavenged from a discontinued toy, chosen for
mass, not quality. Faces judged "recognizable at 2 m in good light,
mood-dependent beyond that."
:::
:::tab{label="Downlink"}
Analog composite video over a 1.2 GHz transmitter — technically requiring
a license the lab technically does not have. Received on the lab's rabbit-
ear CRT, which explains the permanent tinfoil sculpture on the windowsill.
:::
:::tab{label="Footage"}
Flight 4's footage — a spiraling shot of [[akihabara|Akihabara]]'s
skyline, ending in awning — remains the most-rewatched tape in the lab.
It has genuine accidental beauty. It is also evidence, which is why it
stays in the lab.
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="The 'rotor renaissance' plan"}
Daru's revival proposal replaces the AM link with 2.4 GHz proportional
control, doubles the battery, and adds — this is the load-bearing feature —
*a landing mode*. The proposal has been "next month's project" for eleven
consecutive months. It is affectionately tracked on the lab's whiteboard
as #wip and referenced in the [[lab-member-handbook|handbook]]'s section
on scope discipline.
:::

::section[See also]{icon="🔗"}

FG #2's spiritual descendants are everywhere now — see
[[wp:Quadcopter]] for what the industry did with the concept once actual
engineers got involved. Within the lab's canon, the Helicam matters as the
first gadget with a *sensor*: the moment the lab started building things
that observe the world rather than merely gesture at it, a straight line
that runs through the [[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]] to the
[[phone-microwave|PhoneWave]] itself. Not bad for a hat.

# Future Gadget #3: Cyalume Saber

:::infobox{title="FG #3 — Cyalume Saber" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/fg03/300/180" caption="A sword of light, refill sold separately."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Designation | Future Gadget #3 |
| Common name | Cyalume Saber |
| Function | Illuminated prop sword / emergency light source |
| Inventor | [[okabe\|Rintaro Okabe]], blade chemistry by [[daru\|Daru]] |
| Blade | Polycarbonate tube, 78 cm |
| Light source | Chemiluminescent fluid (replaceable cartridge) |
| Burn time | ~40 minutes per cartridge |
| Peak output | ~15 lumens (generous measurement) |
| Structural rating | "Do not actually fence" |
| Status | Functional; cartridge supply intermittent |
:::

**Future Gadget #3**, the **Cyalume Saber**, is a sword-shaped emergency
light: a polycarbonate blade filled with the two-part chemiluminescent
fluid used in glow sticks, ignited — Okabe's verb — by a twist of the hilt
that ruptures the inner cartridge and mixes the reagents. For forty
minutes thereafter, the bearer holds a softly teal sword that cannot cut,
burn, or meaningfully illuminate, and is nonetheless the most-borrowed
gadget the [[future-gadget-lab|lab]] has ever produced.

::section[Chemistry]{icon="🧪"}

::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
:::column
The blade's glow is standard peroxyoxalate chemiluminescence: hydrogen
peroxide oxidizes a diphenyl oxalate ester, and the reaction energy
excites a fluorescent dye that emits as it relaxes. No filament, no
battery in the blade itself, no heat worth mentioning — the reaction runs
at room temperature, which is the entire reason it can live inside a
sealed plastic sword without the sword becoming a hazard.

[[daru|Daru]]'s contribution was the **cartridge**: a glass ampoule of
peroxide suspended in the ester-dye mix, sized so a hilt-twist snaps it
cleanly. Refills are hand-filled at the lab bench with fluid bought in
bulk from a party supplier in [[akihabara|Akihabara]], at a unit cost
[[mayuri|Mayuri]]'s ledger records as "cheaper than snacks, brighter than
nothing."
:::
:::column
**Dye options**

- Teal (canonical)
- Red ("Sith mode," Daru)
- Yellow #stub — reacts too fast,
  burns out in 9 minutes
- Ultraviolet — invisible, philosophically
  troubling, discontinued
:::
::::

::section[Performance]{icon="📊"}

| Metric | Cartridge v1 | Cartridge v2 | Party glow stick (control) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burn time (min) | 24 | 40 | 55 |
| Peak output (lm) | 9 | 15 | 6 |
| Time to peak (s) | 30 | 12 | 45 |
| Cold weather loss | 60% | 35% | 40% |
| Cost per burn (¥) | 180 | 120 | 100 |

The v2 cartridge's ==15 lumens== deserves context: it is brighter than any
commercial glow stick and dimmer than every flashlight ever sold. In a
blackout it renders a room "navigable but melancholy." At a convention it
photographs beautifully. These are, the lab has concluded, the correct
priorities.

:::tip
Twisting the hilt *slowly* mixes the reagents unevenly, producing a blade
that glows in drifting bands — unintended, unfixable, and by broad
agreement the best thing the gadget does. Lab members call the effect
==worldline marbling==, because of course they do.
:::

::section[Service history]{icon="⚔️"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="The blackout"}
During the building-wide power failure that also felled the
[[braun-tube-workshop|CRT shop]] downstairs, three ignited Sabers lit the
lab's stairwell for the duration. This is the gadget's only unambiguous
operational success and it is cited constantly.
:::
:::tab{label="Comima duels"}
Convention choreography revealed the structural rating's meaning: two
Sabers meeting at speed produce one Saber and one teal spill. The fluid is
nontoxic and stains everything. See the [[may-queen-nyan-nyan|May
Queen]]'s tablecloth, which still fluoresces under UV.
:::
:::tab{label="Ceremonial"}
A Saber is ignited at every lab member induction — a tradition begun at
member #004's swearing-in and maintained since, cartridge supply
permitting. The [[lab-member-handbook|handbook]] lists it under
"obligations, non-negotiable."
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="Why not LEDs?"}
An LED blade would be brighter, rechargeable, and permanent — and was
vetoed by Okabe on the record: *"A sword that can be switched off is a
prop. A sword that dies in forty minutes is a story."* The lab notebook
preserves a rebuttal from [[kurisu|Kurisu]] consisting of the word
"battery" underlined four times, then, in different ink, "…fine, it's a
story."
:::

::section[See also]{icon="🔗"}

The underlying reaction is documented at [[wp:Glow stick]]; the lab's
cartridge design adds nothing to the chemistry and everything to the
theater. FG #3 sits between the [[future-gadget-01|Bit Particle Cannon]]'s
pure pageantry and the [[future-gadget-04|Moad Snake]]'s pure utility —
the first gadget where the joke and the function are the same thing. A
proposed two-handed variant, the [[cyalume-claymore|Cyalume Claymore]],
exists only as a red link and a whiteboard sketch of Daru holding it.

# Future Gadget #4: Moad Snake

:::infobox{title="FG #4 — Moad Snake" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/fg04/300/180" caption="A humidifier that commits to the bit."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Designation | Future Gadget #4 |
| Common name | Moad Snake |
| Function | Articulated desktop mist humidifier |
| Inventors | [[daru\|Itaru Hashida]] (mechanism), [[okabe\|Okabe]] (identity) |
| Form factor | 60 cm segmented gooseneck, snake-headed |
| Mist output | 120 mL/hour |
| Reservoir | 900 mL (body coils) |
| Noise floor | 22 dB(A) |
| Named after | A typo that was never corrected |
| Status | In continuous service |
:::

**Future Gadget #4**, the **Moad Snake**, is a desktop ultrasonic
humidifier built into an articulated gooseneck shaped — deliberately,
lovingly — like a snake. The head aims; the coiled body is the water
reservoir; the mist emerges from the mouth in slow, dramatic curls. It is
the only Future Gadget in *continuous daily service* at the
[[future-gadget-lab|lab]], where Tokyo winters and a room full of CRTs
otherwise produce air with the humidity of a kiln.

::section[The name]{icon="🔤"}

The gadget was to be called the **Mood Snake**, for the ambience. The
label maker had other plans. By the time anyone noticed, "Moad" was
painted on the chassis, written in the lab ledger, and — decisively —
funnier. A retroactive backronym was commissioned and the winning entry,
==**M**ist **O**riented **A**mbience **D**evice==, is now the official
line whenever anyone asks, which they always do.[^1]

::section[Mechanism]{icon="⚙️"}

::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
:::column
An ultrasonic transducer at the base of the throat oscillates at 1.7 MHz,
shattering the water surface into a cold fog of droplets a few microns
across; a whisper-quiet fan walks the fog up the neck and out the mouth.
The neck's segments are standard loc-line coolant hose, which holds any
pose — the lab's default is "regarding the divergence meter with
suspicion."

The engineering problem worth documenting is **head droop**: a water-
carrying neck gets heavier as the reservoir feeds forward. Daru's fix
routes the feed line through the neck's neutral axis and moves 80% of
reservoir volume into the base coils, dropping the moment on the neck by
two-thirds. FG #4 is thereby the only Future Gadget with a free-body
diagram in its documentation.
:::
:::column
**Poses, canonical**

- Sentinel (default)
- Regarding the [[divergence-meter|meter]]
- Dramatic S-curve (visitors)
- Down-periscope (storage)
- "Do not disturb" (aimed at door)
:::
::::

::section[Specifications]{icon="📐"}

| Parameter | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Transducer frequency | 1.7 MHz | Standard mist module |
| Droplet size | ~3 µm | Measured by "looks right" |
| Mist output | 120 mL/h | Continuous duty |
| Reservoir | 900 mL | 7.5 h runtime |
| Power | 24 W | Wall adapter, tail-mounted |
| Noise | 22 dB(A) | Quieter than the fridge |
| Segments | 31 | Loc-line, 13 mm |

:::note
The mist is *cold* — ultrasonic humidification adds no heat. First-time
visitors who put a hand in the "snake's breath" expecting warmth
invariably flinch, a reaction the lab logbook tracks under the heading
"Moad bites" (current count: 34).
:::

::section[Service record]{icon="🗓️"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Winter duty"}
Runs 8+ hours daily from November through March. Credited by
[[daru|Daru]] with ending the static-shock feud of the lab's first
winter, in which every doorknob was a betrayal.
:::
:::tab{label="CRT stewardship"}
[[braun-tube-workshop|Mr. Braun]] borrowed FG #4 for a week to test
whether humidified air reduced dust attraction on his shop's tube faces.
Results: inconclusive on dust, conclusive on ambience. He built his own
copy rather than admit he wanted one.
:::
:::tab{label="Incidents"}
One (1): a lab member repositioned the head mid-fill and irrigated the
[[ibn-5100|IBN 5100]]'s bench from 60 cm. The IBN, sealed like a
battleship, was unharmed. The incident report is one sentence: "The snake
was aimed; the snake discharged."
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="Kurisu's assessment"}
[[kurisu|Kurisu]]'s lab-notebook review, quoted in full: "It's a
humidifier. It works. The snake adds nothing." Appended below in Okabe's
hand: "The snake adds *everything*." Appended below that, in Kurisu's,
after a visible gap: "…the snake adds something."
:::

::section[See also]{icon="🔗"}

Ultrasonic humidification is covered at [[wp:Humidifier]]. FG #4 marks the
lab's quiet maturation: after the [[future-gadget-01|Cannon]]'s theater
and the [[future-gadget-02|Helicam]]'s ambition, gadget #4 simply *works*,
every day, at the one job it has — a standard later gadgets are measured
against and mostly fail. Its only rival for practicality is the
[[phone-microwave|gadget that broke causality]], and that one caused
measurably more trouble.

![Sentinel pose](https://picsum.photos/seed/fg04-pose/230/150 "Sentinel pose, mist at full curl.")
:::

[^1]: The runner-up, "Massively Overengineered Aqueous Dragon," lost on
    the technicality that snakes are not dragons. The vote was closer
    than it should have been.

# Future Gadget #5: Kerberos Tap

:::infobox{title="FG #5 — Kerberos Tap" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/fg05/300/180" caption="Three heads. One leash. Guards the underworld of the lab's wiring."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Designation | Future Gadget #5 |
| Common name | Kerberos Tap |
| Function | Voice-commanded three-way power strip |
| Inventors | [[daru\|Daru]] (electronics), [[okabe\|Okabe]] (mythology) |
| Channels | 3 relays × 1500 W |
| Wake word | "Kerberos!" (non-negotiable) |
| Recognition accuracy | 71% (lab ambient), 12% (Comima ambient) |
| Vocabulary | 9 commands |
| Response latency | 0.8 s plus dramatic pause |
| Status | In service, main bench |
:::

**Future Gadget #5**, the **Kerberos Tap**, is a voice-controlled power
strip: three switched outlets, one salvaged speech-recognition module, and
a name that recasts flipping a relay as commanding the hound of Hades.
Shout *"Kerberos! First head, wake!"* and the
[[phone-microwave|PhoneWave]]'s bench light comes on. Shout it again
slightly differently and, 29% of the time, nothing happens, which the
[[future-gadget-lab|lab]] has agreed to call "the hound's discretion."

::section[Origin]{icon="📜"}

::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
:::column
The Tap exists because the lab's main bench accumulated three devices
whose plugs live behind the [[ibn-5100|IBN 5100]] — a machine that weighs
25 kg and does not move for anyone's convenience. After the third
bench-diving expedition in one week, [[daru|Daru]] wired three relays to
a discontinued voice-recognition doorbell chip he'd bought years earlier
"for exactly this kind of emergency."

[[okabe|Okabe]]'s contribution came at naming time. A three-outlet strip
is a three-headed guardian; a three-headed guardian is Kerberos; and a
power strip named Kerberos requires — *requires* — that commands be
delivered as invocations. The syntax stuck because it works: the
recognizer's accuracy is measurably higher on Okabe's declaimed
==\"KERBEROS!\"== than on anyone's normal speaking voice, a fact Daru
has verified, resents, and cannot explain.
:::
:::column
**Command vocabulary**

- "First/Second/Third head, wake"
- "First/Second/Third head, sleep"
- "All heads, wake"
- "All heads, sleep"
- "Guard" — all off after 60 s
  (the "leaving the lab" command)
:::
::::

::section[Specifications]{icon="📐"}

| Parameter | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Relay channels | 3 | 1500 W each, audible *clunk* |
| Recognition chip | HM2007-derivative | Trained per-speaker |
| Vocabulary slots | 12 (9 used) | 3 reserved "for the future" |
| Wake-word accuracy | 94% | The one thing it hears reliably |
| Full-command accuracy | 71% | Lab-quiet conditions |
| False triggers | ~2/month | See incident table |
| Standby draw | 1.1 W | The hound never sleeps |

:::warning
Channel relays are mechanical and loud by design — Daru wanted
unambiguous physical confirmation, having read enough SERN archive
material to distrust silent switching forever. The *clunk* is audible
through the floor in the [[braun-tube-workshop|Braun Tube Workshop]],
whose proprietor has learned to interpret the lab's day from its rhythm.
:::

::section[Incident log]{icon="📋"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="False triggers"}
Documented causes include: a TV documentary about Greek mythology; a
customer downstairs sneezing with unusual commitment; and
[[mayuri|Mayuri]] reading a picture book aloud, which powered down the
soldering iron mid-joint. The phrase "care-bear-os" is now banned in the
lab under statute #wip.
:::
:::tab{label="The rice cooker summit"}
For one winter the third head fed a rice cooker, making "Kerberos! Third
head, wake!" the lab's lunch bell. Decommissioned after the cooker's own
electronics interpreted a brownout as a menu change and produced what the
log calls "congee, adversarial."
:::
:::tab{label="Comima demo"}
At 12% accuracy in convention noise, the demo devolved into Okabe
shouting mythology at an unresponsive power strip for four minutes —
which drew a bigger crowd than any working demo the lab has run.
Three people asked where to buy one. Validation, again.
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="Kurisu's security review"}
[[kurisu|Kurisu]]'s notebook entry: "It's a relay board with a doorbell
chip. Anyone in earshot can command it. Your threat model is 'roommates.'"
Daru's appended rebuttal: "Threat model is *bench ergonomics*, and the
hound has never once made me move the IBN." No further review was filed.
The exchange is preserved in the [[lab-member-handbook|handbook]] as the
canonical example of requirements disagreement.
:::

::section[See also]{icon="🔗"}

The speech chip's lineage is documented at
[[wp:Speech recognition]]; the mythology at [[wp:Cerberus]]. Within the
FG line, the Tap continues the [[future-gadget-04|Moad Snake]]'s quiet
doctrine — a real tool wearing a costume — and its three reserved
vocabulary slots are the lab's most honest roadmap: capacity for the
future, contents unknown. A proposed fourth relay ("the head Hades
removed") is tracked as the red link
[[kerberos-tap-fourth-head|fourth head proposal]].

:::

# Gel Banana Phenomenon

:::infobox{title="Gel Banana" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/gelnana/300/180" caption="Exhibit A. Still attached to the bunch. Still wrong."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Type | Physical anomaly |
| First observed | [[phone-microwave\|Phone Microwave]] trial #4 |
| Subject | One banana (subsequently: many bananas) |
| Result state | Uniform green gel, structurally intact shape |
| Temperature | Ambient (never heated) |
| Weirdest property | Gelled banana found *reattached* to its bunch |
| Explanation | Partial temporal displacement |
| SERN equivalent | "Jellification" — see [[sern-lhc\|Z Program]] |
| Edibility | Formally unresolved; practically, no |
| Specimens retained | 3 (sealed, labeled, avoided) |
:::

The **Gel Banana Phenomenon** is the [[future-gadget-lab|lab]]'s first
piece of experimental evidence that the [[phone-microwave|Phone
Microwave]] was doing something to causality rather than to lunch. A
banana placed in the modified microwave during a phone-linked cycle
emerged transformed: its shape preserved, its substance converted to a
uniform, faintly translucent green gel — **at room temperature**, with no
cooking odor and no measurable heating. The lab's initial classification,
"failed food experiment," survived exactly until someone noticed the
second impossibility: ==the gelled banana was back on its bunch==, across
the room, reattached at the stem.

::section[The observation]{icon="🔍"}

::::columns{ratio="60-40"}
:::column
Reconstruction from the lab notebook: a banana was placed in the drum as
improvised organic ballast during a phone-mode test. The cycle ran nine
seconds. The drum was empty afterward — noted at the time as "banana
misplaced??" — and the bunch on the table, purchased that morning, had
regrown its missing member as gel.

The sequence matters. The banana did not gel in the microwave; it
**vanished** from the microwave and **appeared, gelled, in the past
position it had occupied** before being picked from the bunch. The gel is
what a thing looks like after being sent backward in time *as matter*,
approximately one room and one hour, by a machine tuned for neither.
[[kurisu|Kurisu]]'s later analysis put it flatly: the PhoneWave's first
successful transmission wasn't a D-Mail. It was fruit.
:::
:::column
**Trial tally (bananas)**

- Gelled and relocated: 7
- Gelled in place: 2
- Unaffected: 3
- Vanished entirely: 1 #stub
  (unresolved; do not ask Daru)
:::
::::

::section[Properties of the gel]{icon="🧪"}

| Property | Measurement | Method |
|---|---|---|
| Color | Uniform green, banana-skin hue *throughout* | Visual |
| Consistency | Firm gel; holds shape; cleaves cleanly | Chopstick, sacrificial |
| Temperature at discovery | 22.1 °C (ambient) | IR thermometer |
| Mass vs. original | −4.2% | Kitchen scale |
| Cell structure | None detectable | Daru's USB microscope |
| Odor | Faint banana, "wrong direction" (Mayuri) | Uncontrolled panel |
| Decay behavior | Does not brown; desiccates to resin | 3-week observation |

:::danger
The −4.2% mass deficit has never been accounted for. Applying $E = mc^2$
to 4.2 grams of banana yields $3.8 \times 10^{14}$ joules — which
manifestly did *not* deposit in the lab, or there would be no lab, no
[[akihabara|Akihabara]], and a substantially different wiki. Where the
mass went is the phenomenon's real open question, and the lab's file on
it is titled "DO NOT SOLVE THIS BY EXPERIMENT."
:::

::section[Significance]{icon="⚖️"}

The gel bananas are the hinge of the lab's whole story: the moment its
output changed from [[future-gadget-01|toys]] to evidence.

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Scientific"}
First reproducible temporal displacement of matter by the lab — and a
perfect miniature of [[sern-lhc|SERN's]] "jellification" wall. Matter goes
back; matter arrives *wrong*. The lab reached in nine seconds and one
banana the conclusion SERN's archives reach across three decades and
fourteen human subjects, which is either a triumph of small science or
the darkest data-efficiency argument on record.
:::
:::tab{label="Strategic"}
Recognizing the gel as SERN's jellification is what let [[kurisu|Kurisu]]
redirect the lab toward information-only payloads — the insight that made
[[d-mail|D-Mail]] work. Every worldline shift documented on this wiki
descends from someone looking at ruined fruit and taking it seriously.
:::
:::tab{label="Culinary"}
[[daru|Daru]] ate a spoonful of specimen #2 before the significance was
understood. He reports the taste as "banana, but like it's *remembering*
banana." No effects. He does not discuss it further, and the incident is
the reason the handbook has a rule zero. See
[[lab-member-handbook#rule-zero|Rule Zero]].
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="Specimen inventory"}
Three specimens persist in sealed jars on the lab's anomaly shelf, dated
and initialed. Specimen #1 has desiccated into a translucent resin the
color of old glass; #2 (bitten) is quarantined in a second, angrier jar;
#3 remains gel-state and is the control nobody controls for anything.
The [[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]] sits on the same shelf, which
[[mayuri|Mayuri]] arranged deliberately: "the warnings should live
together." #lore
:::

::section[See also]{icon="🔗"}

For the phase-of-matter background the gel cheerfully violates, see
[[wp:Gel]]. The phenomenon's grown-up siblings are documented under
[[sern-lhc|SERN's Z Program]] (the same failure at human scale) and
[[phone-microwave|Phone Microwave]] (the machine that did it). The lab's
one attempt to reproduce the effect *deliberately* — trial #13, the
vanished banana — is the subject of the unwritten page
[[trial-13|Trial 13]], which no lab member has volunteered to author.

![Anomaly shelf](https://picsum.photos/seed/gelnana-shelf/230/150 "The anomaly shelf. Left to right: warning, warning, warning, clock.")
:::

# IBN 5100

:::infobox{title="IBN 5100" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/ibn5100/300/180" caption="A 1975 portable computer worth more than the building it sits in."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Manufacturer | IBN Corporation |
| Released | 1975 |
| Class | Portable (luggable) personal computer |
| Mass | ~25 kg ("portable") |
| CPU | Custom 16-bit PALM-architecture processor |
| Display | 5-inch monochrome CRT, 64 × 16 characters |
| Storage | Quarter-inch cartridge tape, 204 KB |
| Languages | BASIC, APL |
| Hidden feature | Undocumented multibyte decoding routine |
| Significance | Only machine able to decode SERN's archived LHC reports |
| Known units in Akihabara | One (worldline-dependent) |
| Current owner | [[future-gadget-lab\|Future Gadget Laboratory]] (briefly) |
:::

The **IBN 5100** is a 1975 luggable computer of no particular distinction —
except for one undocumented capability that made a forty-year-old machine
the most contested object in [[akihabara|Akihabara]]: it is the only
computer that can read the archaic multibyte encoding SERN used for its
earliest internal reports. Anyone wanting to read what SERN's archives say
about time travel needs an IBN 5100 first. This includes, at various
points, SERN itself, a round-up of internet conspiracy theorists, and the
[[future-gadget-lab|Future Gadget Laboratory]].

::section[Why it matters]{icon="🗝️"}

::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
:::column
When [[daru|Daru]] first breached SERN's internal network, the juiciest
directories — decades of reports filed under a project name that translates
loosely to "Z Program" — turned out to be stored in a dead encoding no
modern toolchain could parse. Not encrypted: *encoded*, in a proprietary
interchange format IBN shipped briefly in the mid-1970s and documented
nowhere public.

The IBN 5100's firmware contains a translation routine for exactly this
format. IBN never advertised it; the routine appears to have been a
contractual deliverable for a single large customer, and the machine's
service manual refers to it only as "extended interchange support." Whether
that single large customer was SERN is the kind of question that gets a
wiki page flagged #lore, but the circumstantial case writes itself.
:::
:::column
**The chain of need**

Daru's hack → unreadable archives → need IBN 5100 → search
[[akihabara|Akiba]] → [[yanabayashi-shrine|shrine donation]] →
decode → regret. See [[episode-05|Episode 05]] onward.
:::
::::

```mermaid
graph TD;
SERNArchive-->LegacyEncoding;
LegacyEncoding-->IBN5100;
IBN5100-->DecodedReports;
```

::section[The Akihabara unit]{icon="🏮"}

Exactly one unit was known to survive in Akihabara, donated years ago to
the [[yanabayashi-shrine|Yanabayashi Shrine]] and kept in storage as an
offering nobody knew what to do with. The lab's acquisition of it — and the
worldline shifts that repeatedly *un*-acquired it — form one of the
stranger subplots of the lab's first summer. On some worldlines the machine
was never donated at all; on at least one it was destroyed in the 1990s. Its
presence or absence became an informal marker for which
[[alpha-worldline|Alpha worldline]] the lab was currently on, a job later
done properly by the [[divergence-meter|Divergence Meter]].

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Serial number | 5100-J-04471 |
| Condition | Working; CRT slightly burned |
| Shrine storage duration | ~10 years |
| Retrieval attempts | 3 (two undone by worldline shifts) |
| Final disposition | Worldline-dependent |

:::warning
If you have found what you believe to be an IBN 5100 at a flea market,
==do not post about it publicly==. This advice is offered without further
explanation. See [[episode-08|Episode 08]] for what happens to people who
don't take it.
:::

::section[Technical specifications]{icon="📐"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Hardware"}
A single-board design around IBN's PALM processor, executing an
interpreter in microcode: the machine runs BASIC and APL *natively* in the
sense that its "machine language" is itself emulated. This baroque design
is precisely why the decoding routine survives — it lives in the microcode
ROM, not on replaceable media.
:::
:::tab{label="I/O"}
Quarter-inch tape cartridges, a 5-inch internal CRT, and an external video
jack. Daru interfaced it to a modern network by wiring the video output to
a capture card and pointing OCR software at the result — a solution he
describes as "warcrime-adjacent, but shipping."
:::
:::tab{label="Emulation"}
The PALM microcode has never been fully dumped; emulators reproduce the
BASIC environment but not the interchange decoder. As of this writing the
physical machine remains irreplaceable.
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="Collector's market notes"}
Working 5100s trade hands for figures that would fund the lab for a year.
The [[radio-kaikan|Radio Kaikan]] retro-computing floor lists one perhaps
once a decade; the last public listing was withdrawn within four hours
under circumstances nobody at the shop will discuss. Rumors of a second
Akihabara unit surface annually and have never survived contact with a
camera.[^1]
:::

::section[See also]{icon="🔗"}

:::figure{align="left" width="240"}
![Cartridge tape](https://picsum.photos/seed/ibn-tape/240/150 "A 204 KB cartridge. The complete SERN Z Program index fits on six of these.")
:::

The real-world machine this article shamelessly resembles is documented at
[[wp:IBM 5100]]. Within this wiki, the IBN 5100's story is inseparable
from [[sern-lhc|SERN's LHC archives]], the shrine that sheltered it, and
[[okabe|Okabe]]'s repeated attempts to keep it in one worldline long
enough to finish a decode job. A planned page on the
[[palm-architecture|PALM architecture]] has not been written yet.

[^1]: The one photograph that allegedly exists shows, on close inspection,
    a beige sewing machine.

| Payload medium | Bananas (early trials), text message metadata (later trials) |
| Effective range | Confirmed up to several decades; theoretical limit unknown |
| Known side effect | Localized worldline divergence |
| First success | Episode-linked to [[episode-01\|Episode 01]] |
| Current status | Decommissioned after Steins Gate worldline was reached |
| Danger class | #lore ==Restricted-use== |
:::

The **Phone Microwave**, universally shortened to **PhoneWave** by lab members
despite [[okabe|Okabe]]'s insistence on its full parenthetical name, is
[[future-gadget-lab|Future Gadget Laboratory]]'s eighth invention and the
device responsible for the entire plot of the lab's involvement with SERN.
It began as a failed attempt to fax organic matter and ended as the world's
first confirmed **D-Mail** transmitter — a machine capable of sending short
text messages into the past.

Its existence is the reason [[kurisu|Kurisu Makise]] first crossed paths with
the lab, the reason SERN dispatched surveillance and worse, and the reason
[[daru|Daru]] still refuses to eat bananas that have gone soft in a
microwave. See [[episode-guide]] for the episode-by-episode fallout.

::section[Development]{icon="🛠️"}

::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
:::column
The PhoneWave began life as an ordinary microwave oven purchased secondhand
for the lab's kitchenette. [[okabe|Okabe]] — convinced that "phone" and
"microwave" sounded like a suitably mad-scientist combination — rewired it
to accept a mobile handset docked in its drum, with the stated goal of
transmitting matter as a fax machine transmits paper. Early trials only
succeeded in liquefying bananas into a green paste the lab nicknamed
"Gel Banana," a #stub result that nonetheless proved *something* was
crossing between the microwave and the handset.

The breakthrough came after [[kurisu|Kurisu]] joined the lab and picked the
device apart. Her analysis reframed the gel bananas not as a failed
teleportation but as a **partial success**: the microwave wasn't moving
matter through space, it was scrambling a message through *time*. Once the
lab stopped trying to send solid objects and started sending SMS text
instead, the results became reproducible. Okabe rebranded the successful
configuration a "D-Mail," and the age of retroactive causality began.
:::
:::column
**Timeline of note**

- Gel Banana incident — first anomaly
- Kurisu's teardown — reclassifies device
- First successful D-Mail — text-only payload
- SERN surveillance begins shortly after
:::
::::

::section[Working principle]{icon="🔬"}

The PhoneWave does not "send" a message across time in any conventional
sense; it re-encodes a signal so that it destructively interferes with
itself along a closed timelike loop, arriving at the receiving handset
*before* it was sent from the transmitting one. The mechanism piggybacks on
microwave-band emissions and a commercial mobile phone's transceiver — which
is why an unmodified [[ibn-5100|IBN 5100]]-class capacitor bank was later
added to stabilize the packet once payloads grew longer than 148 characters.

```mermaid
graph TD;
PhoneMicrowave-->DMail;
DMail-->PastHandset;
PastHandset-->WorldlineShift;
```

The stored energy required for a single transmission is modest by
laboratory standards. Treating the discharge capacitor as an ideal
capacitor of capacitance $C$ charged to potential $V$, the energy budget is

$$E = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$$

which the lab measured at roughly 40 joules per successful D-Mail — enough,
Daru joked, "to toast half a bagel, or unmake a friendship."

::section[Modes of operation]{icon="⚙️"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Microwave mode"}
Functions as an unremarkable microwave oven. Used daily by lab members for
lunch, with the explicit house rule that nothing metallic goes in the drum
while the phone dock is active — a rule broken exactly once, memorably.
:::
:::tab{label="Phone mode"}
The docked handset receives a call routed through the internal modem. If the
call connects to a phone that existed in the past, the audio (later, SMS
text) reaching that older handset becomes a D-Mail. The sender hears
nothing; there is no dial tone, no ring — only silence and, later, a
notification on a phone that already existed.
:::
:::tab{label="Failure mode"}
Interrupting a transmission mid-cycle — by removing the handset or cutting
power — produces the Gel Banana effect on whatever is in the drum. The lab
keeps a running, unfunny tally.
:::
::::

:::warning
Every confirmed D-Mail shifted the observed [[divergence-meter|reading]] by
a measurable amount. The lab's early messages were sent with no
understanding of how small a change could cascade — see
[[alpha-worldline]] and [[beta-worldline]] for what happens when it does.
:::

::section[Sent D-Mails]{icon="📮"}

:::collapse{title="Known temporal side effects (spoiler-adjacent)"}
Repeated use showed that memories of the "old" worldline can persist in some
individuals even after a shift — a phenomenon later formalized elsewhere as
a Reading Steiner-type effect. The lab does not fully understand why some
members retain memories and others don't; [[kurisu]]'s notes on the subject

:::

# Reading Steiner

:::infobox{title="Reading Steiner" image="https://picsum.photos/seed/rsteiner/300/180" caption="Everyone else's yesterday is negotiable. His isn't."}
| | |
|---|---|
| Type | Cognitive phenomenon |
| Effect | Retains memories across worldline shifts |
| Confirmed bearer | [[okabe\|Rintaro Okabe]] |
| Partial cases | 2 suspected, unconfirmed |
| Named by | Okabe (obviously) |
| Onset sensation | Brief vertigo; "the world blinks" |
| Scientific status | Unexplained |
| Strategic value | The lab's only worldline-shift detector besides the [[divergence-meter\|meter]] |
| Cost | Bearer alone remembers erased events |
:::

**Reading Steiner** is the name [[okabe|Okabe]] gave to his own anomalous
ability: when a worldline shift occurs, his memories do not update with
the rest of the universe. Everyone else seamlessly inherits the new
history, complete with adjusted memories, photographs, and lunch receipts;
Okabe keeps the old ones. He experiences a shift as a lurch of vertigo —
"the world blinks" — followed by the slow, cold discovery of everything
that is now different and always has been.

Without Reading Steiner there would be no wiki page for anything in this
category, because ==no one would know any of it had happened==. Every
D-Mail's before-and-after, every undone timeline documented here, survives
in exactly one place that isn't a Nixie tube. #lore

::section[Phenomenology]{icon="🌀"}

::::columns{ratio="65-35"}
:::column
A shift, from inside Okabe's head: momentary dissociation (reported
duration under two seconds), a sensation he describes as the visual field
"tearing sideways without moving," then continuity — except the room may
have changed, the person he was speaking to may be elsewhere, may not know
him, or may never have existed. The old worldline's memories remain vivid
and do not fade faster than ordinary memory.

The ability triggers on every confirmed shift, with **no known off
switch**. This is documented in the lab notebook as a disability as much
as a gift: after the worst stretch of the lab's first summer, Okabe
experienced fifteen shifts in under a month and retained coherent,
sequential memories of ==several timelines in which a lab member died==.
The [[lab-member-handbook|handbook]]'s rule that no one undertakes
shift-heavy operations alone dates from that month.
:::
:::column
**Shift sensations, logged**

- Vertigo — 100% of shifts
- Nausea — large shifts only
- Sideways "tear" — 80%
- Déjà vu inversion — described
  once, never explained
- Headache — correlates with
  divergence delta
:::
::::

::section[Partial and edge cases]{icon="🧩"}

| Case | Evidence | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| [[okabe\|Okabe]] | Full recall, every shift, corroborated by [[divergence-meter\|meter]] photos | Confirmed |
| [[kurisu\|Kurisu]] | Fragmentary déjà vu; once completed Okabe's sentence about an erased event | Suspected partial |
| [[mayuri\|Mayuri]] | Recurring dreams matching erased timelines; wakes distressed near old convergence dates | Suspected partial |
| [[daru\|Daru]] | None; aggressively normal | Baseline |
| Future visitor | Claimed full RS; unverifiable | Unresolved |

:::note
The partial cases cluster around **emotionally extreme** erased events,
suggesting whatever carries memory across a shift couples to salience
rather than recency. [[kurisu|Kurisu]]'s marginal note: "or the brain
reconstructs from the same cues twice and we're pattern-matching grief.
Both hypotheses fit. One is kinder."
:::

::section[Hypotheses]{icon="🔬"}

::::tabs
:::tab{label="Neurological"}
Something in the bearer's brain fails to participate in the shift —
a defect, in the same sense a surge protector is a defective wire.
Predicts RS should be detectable on imaging. It isn't, or the lab lacks
the machine that could.
:::
:::tab{label="Informational"}
Memory is state; a shift is a state overwrite; RS is a failed write. The
[[sern-lhc|SERN archives]]' memo speculating about "memory-carrier
transfer" reads uncomfortably like an engineering spec for inducing
exactly this. The lab does not enjoy this hypothesis.
:::
:::tab{label="Anthropic"}
Worldlines in which no one remembers shifts contain no one who documents
shifts. A wiki about worldline shifts can only exist downstream of a
Reading Steiner. This is either profound or a tautology, and the lab's
standing vote is 3–3 with one abstention ([[mayuri|Mayuri]], who says it
sounds sad either way).
:::
::::

:::collapse{title="Why 'Reading Steiner'?"}
Okabe has given four contradictory etymologies, involving respectively a
physicist, a mystic, an anagram, and "it came to me in the shift, which
means the worldline itself named it." The lab's official position,
recorded in the handbook glossary: the name is load-bearing nonsense and
must never be changed, as renaming things has historically gone poorly
for this lab.
:::

::section[Operational doctrine]{icon="🛡️"}

Because the bearer is the lab's only shift witness, standing procedure
treats Okabe's testimony as an instrument reading: logged verbatim, dated,
cross-checked against the [[divergence-meter|meter]] photo, never argued
with in the first hour. The doctrine's second clause is the humane one —
after any shift, ==someone sits with him while he lists what changed==,
because the list is the debrief and the debrief is the cost. For the
broader memory-transfer machinery the lab built once RS was understood,
see the [[time-leap-machine|Time Leap Machine]]; for the neuroscience the
lab wishes it had, see [[wp:Memory consolidation]] and the unwritten page
[[salience-coupling|salience coupling]].

![Debrief corner](https://picsum.photos/seed/rs-debrief/240/150 "The debrief corner. Two chairs, one notebook, no arguing.")
:::
